#798. Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model

"Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," the SpaceX CEO said.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big.

The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower.

It was a huge moment for SpaceX, bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship.

"Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines."

The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage.

V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9, SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide.

This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027.

That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height."

So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall.

Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load. Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.November 16, 2026

The original Starship Flight 15 mission plan called for a double chopsticks catch, with both Super Heavy and Ship coming back to the launch tower for recovery.

This would have been feasible, as the catches were scheduled a day apart: Super Heavy would land just 6.5 minutes after launch, while Ship would circle Earth for 22.5 hours, and deploy a batch of SpaceX's Starlink V3 internet satellites, before coming home. (Ship ended up delivering the satellites as planned.)

The twofer didn't happen, however; Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday as a result. But that wasn't a huge deal, as SpaceX had already pulled off Super Heavy catches on three previous Starship flights.

The Ship catch was unprecedented, because it's been a taller order. Ship returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter. SpaceX hadn't even tried the maneuver before Flight 15, so executing it was a very big deal.

"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's Ship-landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

#797. DWTS’ Val Chmerkovskiy Makes Spicy Comment About Jenna Johnson's Exit

Dancing With the Stars pro Val Chmerkovskiy expressed his support for wife Jenna Johnson following their back-to-back eliminations by giving an NSFW shoutout to his “baddie” wife.

Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Johnson may not be adding another Mirrorball to their household, but they're still having a ball at home.

A day after Johnson and her partner Harry Shum Jr. were voted off Dancing With the Stars following his and his partner Jenna Dewan’s elimination the week prior, Chmerkovskiy showed his support for his wife with a steamy comment.

“Keep the trophy’s [sic],” the 40-year-old shared on his Instagram Stories Nov. 18 alongside a photo of Johnson from a red carpet event. “I get to watch this baddie brush her teeth naked every morning.” Chmerkovskiy—who shares son Rome, 3, with his wife of seven years—also thirsted after her by adding a drool emoji.

Johnson and Shum were shockingly sent home on the Nov. 17 semifinals after receiving perfect scores 30 out of 30 for both of their dances: a paso doble to Rihanna's "We Found Love” and a quickstep to Amy Winehouse's “Valerie,” in which Shum paid tribute to late Glee costar Naya Rivera.

While some believe viewers made a major misstep by sending the pair home, the duo slammed the negativity they said they received online, sharing they think it impacted their relationship with the rest of the season 35 cast.

“I hope to get to know them more,” Shum told E! News in an interview following their elimination Nov. 17, “because it's just been so chaotic.”

“We're a bit all trauma bonded,” Johnson chimed in, to which Shum added, “There's a lot of trauma bond just because this year has been a little crazy.”

“Social media is a little nuts,” he continued. “I hope they address that at a certain point, because I think there's a good amount of bullying that doesn't feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it.”

Though Shum didn’t go into specifics, he and Johnson were spun into drama after Chmerkovskiy received a one-week suspension from the show following his now-infamous reaction to a critique judge Carrie Ann Inaba made after one of Johnson and Shum’s performances, in which he referenced Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap.

Shum seemingly referred to the fallout as he praised Johnson after they were voted off.

“I want to say you have been dealing with everything with grace, with the noise outside,” the Grey’s Anatomy star told his partner on air, “and teaching me the things that I have only dreamed of to learn, and this has been one of the most beautiful experiences. So, thank you so much.”

As DWTS prepares to tango into its season 35 finale, read on for a deep dive into the secrets of the ballroom…

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#796. EFL preview: Evans' gripes & unexpected departures

Steve Evans criticised his Bristol Rovers players last week after a disappointing 2-0 loss to Chesterfield left them 18th in the League Two table

The Championship resumes this weekend - but not all will be as it was.

Blackburn Rovers and Swansea City dip their feet into life without Tony Mowbray and Vitor Matos at their sides, for very different reasons.

Meanwhile, Bristol Rovers boss Steve Evans remains in charge in League Two but, given his comments after their last game, it might not be a relationship built to last.

Here are five things to capture your attention this EFL weekend.

Tony Mowbray (right) has left Blackburn Rovers in 13th place in the table while Vitor Matos (left) departs for France with Swansea City in sixth

It would have been a crushing blow to Blackburn fans to lose boss Mowbray, who stepped away due to ill health on Tuesday.

The veteran was surprising the league with a competitive Rovers side only three points away from the top eight and last registering a shock 2-1 win over big dogs West Ham United.

Rovers are not looking for an immediate successor and Mowbray may yet resume his managerial duties at some point, but the side will want to ensure they keep their fine form going rather than leaving him a salvage job to pull off should he return.

To do so, the team will have to put their concerns aside and focus on the job at hand - a Lancashire derby with struggling Burnley at Turf Moor on Sunday (12:00 GMT).

But they are not the only team to be without their trusty manager.

Matos has spread his wings to fly over to Strasbourg and leaves his Swans in a healthy league position but also in poor form.

The Welsh side have lost four of their past five (W1) to begin falling down the pecking order but still remain inside the play-off places, three points below the league leaders and three above West Ham in ninth.

Matos has taken four members of his coaching staff with him, meaning former Swans players Joe Allen and Ashley Williams have stepped in as a makeshift coaching set-up before a difficult game against fifth-placed West Bromwich Albion on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

"Swansea were doing great but I felt they were performing at their absolute maximum," former Stoke full-back Tommy Smith told the 72+ podcast this week.

"I think it's a good opportunity for him, a good opportunity for Strasbourg but it's a tough one for Swansea to take."

Swansea's summer signings 'let down' by Matos

Millwall have won their past three home fixtures against London rivals QPR

Queens Park Rangers boss Julien Stephan believes their London derby against Millwall on Saturday lunchtime (12:30 GMT) will be the first of five games to truly define his side.

The R's are going strong so far this season. They sit inside the play-off positions, five points off the league leaders but it's not enough yet to convince everyone they have finally become promotion contenders after 12 years mostly in the doldrums.

"The thing that is going to hold us back is consistency," QPR fan Gareth Dixon told BBC Radio London.

"We have far too many players injured too frequently. Getting that first, strongest XI is a challenge for us.

"If we can get our strongest team out, if we can keep the performances up then we are looking at top eight."

Millwall, meanwhile, know what it's like to push for a place in the Premier League in recent times, but things have not panned out so well this season.

Injuries have hampered them and after only two wins in their past 10 league games, both against teams in the bottom three, the Lions' season is yet to really get going.

All three of the Championship clubs based in the West Midlands plus Staffordshire's Stoke City are within one point of each other at the top of the table

There is something in the air around the western side of the Midlands.

Only Middlesbrough disrupt a top five of West Midlands and Staffordshire clubs and the two best of that bunch are league leaders Birmingham City and third-placed Stoke City.

Both are on three-match winning streaks and sit on 29 points, separated merely by Blues' superior goal difference.

Saturday's game at the Bet365 Stadium (15:00 GMT) will see the two go head-to-head for a top-two spot - and possibly top spot itself.

But a draw could open the door for either Wolves or West Bromwich Albion to reach the summit instead.

I mean, just look how tight the division is.

Dave Challinor was announced as new Sheffield Wednesday boss on 1 November

In a game against fellow promotion contenders Plymouth Argyle last weekend, Sheffield Wednesday claimed a convincing 3-0 victory to mark Dave Challinor's return to League One management.

Their next opponent, Barnsley, seem like they will be an easier ride. The Tykes have the joint fewest points in the league with nine, kept off the bottom through goal difference alone.

A derby under the lights can produce something special though.

Barnsley have won both their previous matches against Wednesday and will be seeking a third in a row for the first time since 1946.

No one is expecting the Tykes to claim all three points when they meet on Friday night (20:00 GMT) but that means all the pressure is on the rebuilding Wednesday side.

The Owls did not deal so well with that expectation in the two cup games Challinor began his reign with, losing in the FA Cup to Oldham Athletic and suffering a 4-0 drubbing in the EFL Trophy against Accrington Stanley.

Can they rise to the occasion or is it Barnsley's time to get motoring?

Challinor hoping Argyle win is just 'the start'

Few bosses in League Two have the experience of Steve Cotterill and Steve Evans

Cheltenham Town boss Steve Cotterill isn't much loved by the Bristol Rovers fan base.

The 62-year-old led the Gas' local rivals Bristol City to the League One title and the EFL Trophy in 2015, earning the Robins' eternal admiration and Rovers' unrelenting dislike.

However, back at his boyhood club, Cotterill will be aiming to quieten his critics among the away support as he looks to take Cheltenham into the League Two play-off spots when the two sides face each other on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

His current Robins have lost five of their past seven games (W2) but still remain just a point shy of the top seven.

Rovers, meanwhile, are tumbling down the table at a rapid rate after a seven-game winless run where they have taken just one point - and they are hardly putting up a united front.

Manager Steve Evans has suggested he will depart the club if he feels they no longer want his services and has placed blame on his players for their run of poor form.

"You're going to Steve Cotterill's Cheltenham side, who are very good, particularly at Whaddon Road," Evans told BBC Radio Bristol after their loss to Chesterfield last weekend.

"We have to pick a team first and foremost that works hard and fights.

"I'll still turn up at 6.30 in the morning. I'll still leave at 6 o'clock at night. I still go and watch the opposition, do the analysis. What's changed? I know what's changed â inconsistent players."

#795. Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul

The reforms mark a break the the conservative policies of former PM Viktor Orban. The controversial "heartbeat regulation" is to be scrapped and women are to be better protected against violence.

Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.

Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.

Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.

The changes proposed by the new government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.

The country also plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.

The controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.

The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions."

The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.

Hungary also plans to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.

"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only ⁠take ​place with the voluntary consent of the other party," ​Magyar said.

The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology."

"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.

Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

#793. Frank happy to be 'back in the circus' at Palace

Thomas Frank replaces Frenchman Pierre Sage at Crystal Palace

Thomas Frank is happy to be "back in the circus" after speaking at his first news conference as Crystal Palace manager.

The 53-year-old, who was appointed on a two-and-a-half-year deal on Monday, has been out of work since he was sacked by Tottenham in February, less than eight months after taking the job.

But, rather than dwell on that disappointment, Frank hopes to use it as a learning exeprience as he attempts to improve Palace's fortunes and lift them off the bottom of the Premier League table.

"If you don't learn from any of your jobs, I don't think you reflect, I don't think you improve, and I don't think you get better," said Frank.

"Of course there's a lot of things I have been reflecting over. The details, that will be for another time, but I can say I've learned, definitely."

The Dane said he could easily have extended his break from football, which he used to travel to Japan and Australia, as well as "visiting friends and family, eating too well [and] drinking too much wine" back in his homeland.

"I was very aware I didn't want to do anything in the summer. I put a statement out there, I needed more time," he added.

"I can actually, honestly say I would have been fine if it was three, four, five, six, seven months more, because it's good to be back in the circus, but it's also unbelievably good not to be in, especially if you enjoy life, which I do.

"I was spending time with family and friends and doing all that, but I think the club, the way Palace is, how well Steve Parish especially spoke about the club and ideas, Matt Hobbs and Iain Moody and these guys, too, helped convince me it was a good idea.

"I'm a little bit surprised by this feeling I have in the body, how good it feels."

How Frank can restore reputation and save Crystal Palace

Frank's Palace reign begins with a trip to Coventry City on Saturday (15:00 GMT) and he says he returns to the dugout unbruised despite the way his stint at Spurs ended.

"I think we all have an ego," the former Brentford boss said. "Some are better at controlling it than others. For me, it's not the critics, it's more what I can learn, what I can prove, how I can get better.

"There's a lot of clever people out there, but the interesting thing is they only know 10 per cent of the truth. That's a tenth of the truth at Brentford, there's a tenth of the truth at Tottenham, and that's just the way it is.

"If you can't handle that as a coach or a player, then you shouldn't be in this business, and I'm very happy to be back in the game."

#792. Moore eyes Kane shirt as Spurs' past and future stars meet

Moore is Tottenham's youngest-ever Premier League player, having made his debut for the club's senior side at just 16 years old.

Cologne loanee Mikey Moore says he hopes to exchange shirts with former Tottenham team-mate Harry Kane when they face Bayern Munich in the Bundesliga on Friday.

The 19-year-old England Under-21 international is on a season-long loan from Spurs, while Three Lions captain and Ballon d'Or winner Kane left north London to join Bundesliga giants Bayern in 2023.

"I haven't actually spoken to him. When he was leaving Tottenham I was just coming into the first team so we don't really know each other too well," said Moore.

"But we've got Bayern on Friday so I'm looking forward to hopefully getting a chat with him and maybe his top."

The 19:30 GMT kick-off will be shown live on BBC Sport and iPlayer.

Kane was still at Tottenham when Moore was first invited to train with the senior squad during the 2021-22 season.

"He's been a massive idol of mine since I was really young," Moore told the Euro Leagues podcast last month.

"When I first went up to train with the first team under Antonio Conte, Harry Kane was over there, and [I saw] some finishing that [I have] never seen anything like again.

"It will be a great experience to play against him and share a pitch with him."

The pair may not have crossed paths in Germany yet but Moore did bump into the England skipper while on international duty last month.

"I'll try my best to get my hands on that shirt," Moore added. "I saw him on the last international break, actually, and went and said hello.

"Hopefully, I'll be coming back to Koln with that in my hand."

How much German has Mikey Moore learned so far?

Moore says the success of Jadon Sancho and Jude Bellingham in the Bundesliga influenced his decision to join Cologne on loan.

Moore's move came almost a decade after a 17-year-old Sancho left Manchester City to join Borussia Dortmund.

During his time in Germany, Sancho established himself as one of Europe's most exciting wingers, making more than 150 appearances for Dortmund and helping the club win the DFB-Pokal in 2021. He subsequently secured a Â£73m move to Manchester United.

Bellingham followed a similar path in 2020, leaving boyhood club Birmingham City to join Dortmund. The midfielder quickly developed into one of the most sought-after players in world football before joining Real Madrid for an initial Â£88.5m in 2023.

"Over the years you've seen so many young players come out here, and there are good examples of world-class players like Jude Bellingham and Jadon Sancho doing really well," Moore said.

"It's a really attractive place to play football, especially for a young attacker. It's a great platform to play, and that was sold to me by the people at the club and the manager.

"They've put real trust in me, and the amount of game time I've played so quickly in my Koln [Cologne] career has been nice. It's been good to have that trust from all the staff and people at the club.

"I'm already happy with my decision. Now I can really kick on, make my own story and build my own path in German football."

Although Moore only turned 19 in August, he is no stranger to stepping outside his comfort zone.

Last season, he made 47 appearances in all competitions, including the Champions League qualifying rounds, during a loan spell at Scottish Premiership side Rangers.

It was the first time Moore had left his boyhood club Tottenham, and he rose to the challenge, scoring six goals and providing two assists in 28 Scottish Premiership appearances.

The experience offered a different test to the one he now faces in Germany, but it provided valuable exposure to the demands of first-team football.

"I had options to stay in England and maybe stay somewhere a little more comfortable," Moore said.

"But the conversations came down to me picking a team, and I wanted to take myself a little bit out of my comfort zone to test myself in one of the top five leagues.

"When we were speaking, everyone said they thought it would be a really good experience for me to experience this type of football.

"It's really intense, and there are some great teams in the league.

"For me, it was a no-brainer. I made the decision early that I wanted to come out here, and now I just need to push on."

Having now found an apartment close to fellow England youth internationals Reigan Heskey and Jahmai Simpson-Pusey, who also joined the club this summer, the teenager has turned his attention to learning German.

Moore had his first lesson last month and, at his mother's request, is hoping to expand his vocabulary in the language over the coming weeks.

"I wasn't the brightest at school, so I might take a while to learn the language," Moore joked.

"At least I'll be able to learn a few words so I can order my food in German."

#791. Why Dolly Parton’s Niece Danielle Wore Singer’s Dress to CMA Awards

Dolly Parton’s niece Danielle Parton—who is brand ambassador to her estate—attended the 2026 CMA Awards wearing a dress the county legend was meant to wear in the “Light of Clear Blue Morning” video.

A little piece of Dolly Parton was at the 2026 CMA Awards.

Nearly two months after the country music legend died, her niece Danielle Parton—who was named the brand ambassador of Dolly’s estate last month—wore a dress custom-made for the “Jolene” singer.

The all-white, fringe-forward frock was, of course, covered in rhinestones and included a trim of many colors around the low-cut neckline, bodice and skirt. Danielle, 50, paired the look with diamond jewelry and a pair of gold heeled boots at the CMA Awards Nov. 18.

“It was made for the ‘Light of Clear Blue Morning’ video that she never got to finish and get to do,” Danielle told E! News in an exclusive interview on the red carpet. “So I'm wearing it tonight in honor of her.”

And while Dolly’s niece may have been inspired by the “I Will Always Love You” singer’s wardrobe, she quickly found that her aunt Dolly’s words of wisdom have left a far greater impact.

“Almost immediately right after she passed, I gave myself one day to sit around and cry and feel pitiful about it,” Danielle continued. “Then the following day I had stuff to do, and I remember she'd always say, ‘Well, you just got to get your rear in gear and get to it.’ So that's what I did.”

But Danielle knows that Dolly’s impact goes far beyond the Parton family.

“Dolly was such an incredible human,” she said. “I'm a fan of hers as much as I am a family member, and it's always nice, especially as a family member, to see somebody in your own family have a positive impact on other people.”

As for the tribute to Dolly performed by Vince Gill and CMA host Lainey Wilson during the event, Danielle noted she was “really excited to see those that she's had such an influence on get to pay their respects in their way.”

Read on for a roundup of all the country music stars and celebs that boot scoot boogied down the CMA Awards’ red carpet.

#790. Relive Starship's historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and 'Mechazilla' tower catch

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.

Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did.

Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench.

The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies.

Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II, with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away.

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space, while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase.

That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase.

Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball.

This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system.

Ship continued on to low Earth orbit, where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites. It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX says is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite launches worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation.

Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch.

At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower.

After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight.

It hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts.

SpaceX has not yet said whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry.

Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#789. Too late for Jackson? - FPL gameweek 11 dilemmas

The Premier League is back after the international break and BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert Gianni Buttice gives his answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers heading into gameweek 11.

With 33 points in the past three rounds, you might think you've missed your chance to own Aston Villa forward Nicholas Jackson (Â£7.2m). But he remains in superb form, with five excellent fixtures ahead, making him the round's most transferred player once again.

Liverpool have traditionally offered plenty of popular FPL options, but their players have attracted less backing this season. Only Arsenal, Brighton and Leeds have conceded fewer goals, making Jeremy Jacquet (Â£5.1m) an appealing differential with ownership below 5%.

In attack, Alexander Isak (Â£9.3m) is FPL's second among forwards for points scored. Florian Wirtz (Â£7.2m), meanwhile, is beginning to find a new level of consistency for Liverpool, with five attacking returns in his last six matches.

Defensive contribution points have been a welcome addition to FPL and have contributed to the rise of playing a back four. Antonio Silva (Â£5.1m), Tarik Muharemovic (Â£5.1m) and Jan Paul van Hecke (Â£5.1m) are among the best at earning the extra two points, while also offering significant goal threat and playing for strong defensive sides. Bournemouth, Leeds and Tottenham rank among the top five for expected goals conceded, giving these mid-priced centre-backs an unusually wide range of routes to points.

Maxim de Cuyper (5.5m) is a unique case of an out-of-position defender playing in a front three and is therefore a must have.

Is it time to target Spurs players in FPL?

Several popular players enter Gameweek 11 with three or four yellow cards. A fifth booking before their 19th league match will rule them out of their team's next league fixture.

Pascal Gross (Â£6.3m), Marcus Tavernier (Â£6.7m), Antonio Silva (Â£5.1m) are all on four yellows while De Cuyper (5.5m), Morgan Rogers (Â£8.2m) and Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Â£6.0m) are on three.

Many engaged FPL managers see this as the season's most important stretch: 10 gameweeks in 45 days, including several midweek rounds. Injuries, suspensions and rotation make a reliable first substitute essential. Where possible, choose players who regularly complete 90 minutes and rarely miss matches, and consider banking transfers so you can react when availability flags appear in your squad.

#788. What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?

The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.

Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

#787. Key questions as Scottish Premiership returns

Wouter Wrancken under pressure; Mario Frick's beginning; John McGlynn the saviour

The Scottish Premiership returns with an all-action Saturday after what was a bleak international break for the national side.

Most of the intrigue is on men who will not make a pass or a tackle. There is one new manager, one who is being touted for the Scotland job, another who has turned around a failing side and one who is increasingly under pressure.

And none of those are in charge of Old Firm teams. The managerial status at Celtic and Rangers is relatively settled, but of course that can change in the space of 90 minutes.

This is your essential guide to Saturday's action.

Aberdeen have a new head coach for their basement battle with Kilmarnock, with Mario Frick replacing Stephen Robinson

The Liechtensteiner was a fine striker in his day and his main mission is to get the Dons firing in front of goal again.

Frick favoured two up top while in charge of Luzern, so he needs to find a way to supply Kevin Nisbet and Ayoub Mouloua.

Connor Ronan could hold the key to improving a sorry set of attacking statistics, but the Irish midfielder will need to show more than he has since his summer arrival.

Aberdeen have 12 goals from 12 league games. Kilmarnock have 13 from 13. Both sides have amassed just four points from their past six outings, so this may well be something of a scrap.

Killie were slightly more menacing in a 0-0 draw at Pittodrie in September and the same could be said of a League Cup quarter-final at Rugby Park a week later, although the Dons did well to prevail on penalties after a red card early in the second half.

The Ayrshire side have the league's worst defensive record by a distance, conceding three or more goals on six occasions. However, manager Neil McCann will have been heartened by a tenacious showing in the 1-0 loss at Celtic Park last time out.

With four successive matches coming against sides currently in the bottom six before taking on the Dundee duo, McCann will view this pre-Christmas sequence as vital.

Hear from Aberdeen's Mario Frick at first press conference

Of the leading sides, Celtic have the easier-looking task at home to St Mirren, who have enjoyed just one victory in their past 40 visits to the east end of Glasgow in all competitions.

However, the league leaders have not kicked on since thrashing Heart of Midlothian last month, drawing with Dundee United and losing to Falkirk either side of narrow and unconvincing wins over Hibernian and Kilmarnock.

That 1-0 win at home to Killie was just a second clean sheet in seven Premiership matches for the champions.

Celtic came from behind to win 2-1 in Paisley in September, with Yang Hyun-Jun grabbing the second. The winger's return should add dynamism to their attack.

Since pushing Celtic all the way at home, St Mirren have picked up a mere four points from nine matches.

Rangers go to Motherwell off the back of a 2-0 win away to the Buddies, extending their unbeaten league run to 10 games and maintaining the best defensive numbers in the table.

The goals came from a contentious penalty and a deflected shot and manager Derek McInnes spoke of the need to sharpen up in the final third after several promising situations broke down.

After a six-game losing slump that began in Govan, Motherwell have steadied the ship and played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with Dundee United before the break that included a combined 40 efforts on goal.

Well shared the points with Rangers at Fir Park last season, scoring late on both occasions, and, while not the force they were after so many departures, still retain a core of players who celebrated victory at Ibrox in April.

Rangers have the momentum, although recent draws away to Dundee and Hearts underline the fact they remain a work in progress under McInnes.

New manager Frick to take Aberdeen back to basics

We'll only sell if offer makes club blink - McInnes

Five wins on the spin have propelled Falkirk up to third place and they will be big favourites to extend that run at home to St Johnstone.

Celtic beaten, Hearts hammered... fans are talking about European qualification, having ended a five-year stint in League 1 in May 2024.

John McGlynn continues to work his magic on a meagre budget, with new arrivals Jacob Murrell, Owen Eames, Finley Barbrook and Deniss Melniks hitting the ground running.

Ethan Ross is lapping up a new lease of life, while older heads Scott Bain and Liam Henderson have never been better, although the loss of influential skipper Brad Spencer is a huge blow.

The Perth Saints will be no pushovers. They too are punching above their weight with just four defeats in 13 on their return to the top flight.

Rangers are the only side to beat Simo Valakari's men since a 1-1 draw with Falkirk at McDiarmid Park in mid-September.

That was the first league meeting of the clubs since 2010, but, with such astute managers in place, it looks like this can remain a top-flight rivalry for a good while yet.

Have Hibs turned a corner and have Hearts fallen down a hole?

Marink Reedijk lost his first three games after replacing David Gray, but now the Hibs head coach is looking for a third successive victory at home to Dundee United.

The Easter Road side clambered out of the bottom spot in style, thumping Aberdeen 4-0 at Pittodrie after coming from behind to stun their Edinburgh rivals in the League Cup semi-final.

Hearts went into that game at Hampden as heavy favourites and across the following seven days were outplayed by the team sitting eighth in the Swiss Super League and walloped by Falkirk, ending their 19-month long unbeaten home record in the league.

A growing injury list has hampered Hearts, but Wouter Vrancken's methods are being questioned, with only Kilmarnock conceding more goals in the league.

A visit to Dundee is next and Steven Pressley's much-improved team have only been defeated once at Dens Park so far.

United have also been a breath of fresh air, adopting a new swashbuckling style that has yielded four wins and four draws in their past nine games.

Hibs have taken significant strides, particularly in the midfield area, but this will be a real test of their progress. There were 11 goals in the two games against United at Easter Road last season and another big score would not be a surprise.

#786. DWTS' Alfonso Ribeiro Sets Record Straight on Voting Point System

After Dancing With the Stars shockingly eliminated Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson in the semi-finals, host Alfonso Ribeiro chimed in on fan speculation about how the show's ranking system works.

Alfonso Ribeiro has proof that on Dancing With the Stars, the numbers add up.

After a season of nail-biting eliminations, the DWTS host responded to a fan theory stating contestants are ranked twice in numerical order—from highest to lowest—based on their scores from the judges' panel and again from the audience vote. From there, the theory suggests each star is awarded two sets of points to match their numerical positions in each ranking.

But the Fresh Prince of Bel-Air alum shut down the assumption that two stars ranking the same—like when Amber Glenn and Jenna Dewan both earned 30 points from the judges in week nine—would result in skipping the next lowest position altogether, impacting the number of points all lower stars would receive toward escaping elimination.

"Now do the math with no breaks in the scores. It doesn’t skip 5," Ribeiro wrote Nov. 18, referring to how Harry Shum Jr. earning the highest judges' score of the seven contestants ranked him highest at number seven, followed by Glenn and Dewan tying for sixth, while placing Maura Higgins at fifth position instead of fourth. "Maura would get 5. No skip."

And since Ezra Frech, Tatyana Ali and Connor Wood all earned the same lowest score of 27 points that week, Ribeiro again clarified how they would all rank the same, in the next position behind Higgins.

As he explained, "The lowest judges scores might be 4 not 3."

In response to sharing the behind-the-scenes insights, the original poster replied, "Speechless! Ahhh making these adjustments! Thanks Alfonso!"

And it's not the only time the 55-year-old has separated fact from fiction when it comes to the competition series. He also responded to the theory that the show was rigged against certain competitors following Hayes Grier's elimination in season 21.

"No chance," Ribeiro replied to a clip of the LexLos podcast discussing speculation about manipulating the vote. "We want everyone who’s popular to stay on. It’s basic logic."

Read on to learn more about who goes in the ballroom after the cameras go down.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#785. Inside the rise of 'humble' Nyoni and why Iraola trusts him

Trey Nyoni scored his first Liverpool goal earlier this month

Trey Nyoni knew this was the season when opportunity beckoned for him at Liverpool.

With Curtis Jones leaving for Inter Milan and the club deciding not to buy another midfielder, Nyoni saw the prospect of regular first-team action if he impressed new head coach Andoni Iraola in pre-season.

First impressions matter. So on the day he returned from a holiday in Morocco in June, Nyoni went from the airport to a personal training session in Leicester - where the 19-year-old grew up and where his family are still based.

Nyoni sought the help of a private football coaching operation as he targeted off-season gains before joining up again with Liverpool.

Coach Steve Stavrou and his son Emillio have also worked with players including Harvey Barnes and Haji Wright. Nyoni asked to work on line-breaking passes, getting away from pressure and improving his finishing.

"We merely supplemented the ability he's already got. He's a quiet and humble lad but knows his ability on the pitch and plays with such a confidence," Emillio Stavrou tells BBC Sport.

Under Iraola, Nyoni has thrived after a stellar pre-season, making 13 appearances already, just one shy of his total appearances last season.

Earlier this month, he scored his first goal for the club in Istanbul.

Liverpool ultimately lost to Fenerbahce in the Champions League that night and Nyoni's belief that "the night has been ruined" showed his inner competitiveness.

His first Premier League start came against last season's champions Arsenal on 1 November.

Nyoni fouled Arsenal's captain early on, leading one source to remark: "He's a nice kid but you saw that steel too with the way he went into Martin Odegaard."

Perhaps the most significant praise came from Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard, who said he couldn't see why Iraola was taking Nyoni off just before the hour mark in that game.

Iraola was managing Nyoni's workload, with the midfielder playing 85 minutes three days later in Turkey.

By now, it is clear that Iraola is unafraid to use him.

"He has to continue in the same place he has been since pre-season: being ready for every game. He is playing all the games lately - so we trust him," said Iraola.

That speaks volumes of Nyoni's rise since joining from Leicester City in 2023 and making his Liverpool debut under Jurgen Klopp as a 16-year-old.

Nyoni, whose parents have Zimbabwean heritage and support Liverpool, is in advanced talks over a new deal.

Having made his England Under-21 debut last week, this is turning into a breakout season with club and country.

Under Iroala, Nyoni has made six starts for Liverpool

In the summer window, the average spend on a player signed from another Premier League club was Â£39.4m.

Judging by Liverpool's recent signings - the likes of Alexander Isak (Â£125m), Bradley Barcola (Â£123m) and Florian Wirtz (Â£116m) - there is a sense of satisfaction at the club when the likes of Rio Ngumoha and Nyoni, who cost a fraction of those sums, emerge as first-team options for years to come.

A tribunal decided that Liverpool had to pay Chelsea up to Â£6.8m in compensation for Ngumoha. In Nyoni's case, Liverpool paid just under Â£1m in compensation to Leicester.

Nottingham Forest were linked with a Â£30m move for Nyoni in the summer. Forest denied making the bid, while Liverpool were not interested in a sale.

Iraola saw enough over pre-season to know the teenager would play a prominent part in the new campaign. He only got 237 minutes last season under Arne Slot but has already played 619 minutes this time around.

Slot saw the potential of Nyoni, who trained regularly with the first team. But, given Liverpool's struggles in 2025-26, the Dutchman was reluctant to experiment.

Under Iraola, Nyoni is finding his feet in a deeper midfield role than he had been used to, seeing more of the ball.

"I've been playing like a number six. I played there when I was young, but it's a new position for me. I've had to learn a lot in a short space of time," Nyoni told The Inside Scoop., external

The time he spent before pre-season impressed on the coaches there what a talent Nyoni possessed.

"In the drills, he'd make everything game realistic. Everything was with intent and you see a lot of what he does is with disguise, particularly with his passes," Emillio Stavrou recalls.

With two games a week now the norm for Liverpool, Iraola will continue to rotate his team.

But seeing who he names in midfield against Manchester United on Sunday will be interesting because Nyoni is showing that he can fight for a position alongside the likes of Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Alexis Mac Allister.

Inevitably there is work to be done, particularly in terms of endurance and physicality, in order to cope with the rigours of playing consistently at the top level, but it is so far, so good for Nyoni.

Liverpool and Man Utd fans give predictions ahead of Premier League match

In a similar manner to Ngumoha's emergence last season, Liverpool were keen not to block Nyoni's pathway, and under Iraola he has been given the platform to thrive.

Liverpool are still only an injury away from looking short of options, so getting another midfielder remains a priority for next summer.

Monaco's Lamine Camara and Bournemouth's Alex Scott are two players of interest.

In the here and now, Nyoni needed this opening. He has come out of his shell and feels a lot more like a part of the squad. That quiet nature is slowly changing and that was visible in an interview he did while on England duty.

Asked how Liverpool are doing by one of the hosts, who supports Manchester United, Nyoni simply responded: "Better than United."

Deep down, there is a young man that backs himself and by all accounts, loves football. Neymar is his favourite player.

"He's obsessed with training and obsessed with getting better. The first session we had with him after he'd just got off the plane tells you about him," adds Emillio Stavrou.

Nyoni told Stavrou's little brother in the summer that he backed himself to play regularly for Liverpool.

#784. On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

"Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."

Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

"For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn."

For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or New York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies plan to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

#778. Bruno Mars Announces Death of Dad in Heartbreaking Post

Bruno Mars shared that his dad Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74, writing in an emotional tribute, "In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world."

Bruno Mars knows his dad was amazing, just the way he was.

The “That’s What I Like” shared that his father Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74 and shared a heartfelt tribute to the impact he had on his life.

“Last week I got to hug my father one last time,” Mars wrote on Instagram Nov. 19. “If you’ve ever seen me talk about him I’ve always said that he’s the man that taught me everything I know, especially when it comes to music.”

The 41-year-old—whose real name is also Peter Hernandez—added that his father helped raise six children, including Mars, his sisters Tiara, Tahiti, Presley and Jaime and his brother Eric, saying, “In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world, and I will miss him everyday until we meet again.”

Mars—whose mother Bernadette San Pedro Bayot died from a brain aneurysm in 2013 at the age of 55—concluded his message by writing, “I Love you Pops. Kiss mom up there for me.”

Alongside the emotional message, the “Just the Way You Are” singer shared a photo of himself and his father sharing an embrace in a hospital bed along with several pictures of his father from throughout the years. He did not confirm his father’s cause of death.

Mars and his dad had shared a truly special bond through the years as the “Uptown Funk” singer’s love of music was inspired by his father’s own history of performing. While Hernandez was born in Brooklyn, he later moved to Hawaii, where he founded a doo-wop revival group called The Love Notes.

And from a young age, Hernandez—who split from Mars’ mother when the Grammy winner was 12—knew that his son was destined for greatness.

“He was a ham,” Hernandez told MidWeek about Mars in 2014. “As soon as he could walk and express himself, he had to be in the middle of everything and wanted to be a part of whoever he’d seen on TV.”

Of course, he was incredibly proud that his son was “the product of a lot of love from all his family.”

“No woman could ever love Bruno as much as his late mother did,” he added, “and no man could ever love Bruno as much as I love him.”

And Hernandez was there for his son right until the end, offering Mars advice on what to say when he was honored with a Las Vegas street named after him in April.

“He says, ‘My loving son, I know you don't like advice, but getting a street named after you is a monumental moment,’” Mars recounted in a video from the event shared by AP News. “‘I just wanna say, I know you must be very proud, ‘cause I’m so proud for you. If you are gonna say anything on the mic to the crowd, both God and people love humility. So be humble and tell your fans it's their street, and you're so honored and grateful.’”
