#726. A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret. For more than two centuries, scientists believed that the genus Colobura contained just one widespread species. Now, researchers have identified a third species that looks almost identical to its relatives, raising new questions about how these butterflies evolved and continue to live alongside one another.

The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History. By combining DNA analysis with subtle differences in wing patterns and ultraviolet light reflection, the team uncovered distinctions that had remained largely invisible to scientists.

Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time. Yet genetic evidence suggests they remain separate, with no detectable signs of interbreeding.

A Familiar Butterfly With a Hidden Identity

Central and South America's tropical rainforests contain some of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet. Costa Rica alone supports approximately half a million species, roughly five times the number found across Canada, even though Canada's land area is about 200 times larger.

Despite this extraordinary diversity, certain plants and animals are especially recognizable throughout the region. In Canada's boreal forests, balsam firs are a familiar feature of the landscape. In tropical America, trees belonging to the genus Cecropia play a similarly prominent role.

In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper described their importance, writing, "Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember Cecropia, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries."

The butterflies of the genus Colobura are just as recognizable, according to Sapkota.

"If you go to the neotropics, Colobura is one of the first butterflies you see," she said.

These butterflies and Cecropia trees share a close ecological relationship because Cecropia leaves provide food for Colobura caterpillars. Both groups occur across an enormous geographic area, from portions of the Andes Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon to the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay. They are also widespread throughout Central America and the Caribbean Islands.

Such broad distributions are not particularly unusual in tropical ecosystems. However, the diversity within these groups presents an interesting contrast.

Scientists recognize 61 species of Cecropia, many of which occupy relatively small geographic areas. Some grow only in the Andes, while others are confined to the Caribbean.

For Colobura butterflies, the situation appeared very different. After Carl Linnaeus formally described Colobura dirce in 1758, scientists spent more than 200 years treating the genus as a single species, despite its extensive range.

That understanding began to change in 2001, when researchers formally recognized a second species. Now, an unexpected discovery in Venezuela has led to the identification of a third, described by Sapkota and her colleagues in Zootaxa.

Rather than providing a simple explanation for the group's evolutionary history, the discovery has introduced an even greater puzzle.

"It's crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time."

A Butterfly Mystery Dating Back More Than 150 Years

Distinguishing adult Colobura butterflies is exceptionally difficult. Their wings are nearly identical, with only slight variations in a gray stripe on the underside of the front wings. In some butterflies, this stripe becomes a little wider. In others, it stays the same width. It may also extend far enough to meet a yellow band running across the wing, or stop short of it.

Their caterpillars offer somewhat clearer clues.

Colobura caterpillars have velvety black bodies covered with prominent yellow projections that end in sharply angled barbs. These defensive structures send a warning to potential predators that could be interpreted as "leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences."

Beneath those conspicuous spines are much smaller cream-colored markings. Depending on the species, these markings may resemble teardrops or rings, or they may be missing entirely.

The importance of these differences was recognized surprisingly early.

In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp proposed that caterpillars with different cream-colored patterns represented two separate species. Other researchers rejected his interpretation, arguing that the variations could reflect differences between males and females or simply natural variation within a single species.

That view remained dominant for approximately 150 years.

In 2001, Keith Willmott and several colleagues revisited Sepp's observations and formally described a second species, Colobura annulata. Willmott is now a curator at the Florida Museum's McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity.

"We assumed that was the problem solved," Willmott said.

He moved on to other research, believing the longstanding classification problem had been resolved. However, occasional observations continued to suggest that something was missing.

"I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible."

At the time, even the existence of two nearly indistinguishable species seemed remarkable.

"It's a very distinctive butterfly. It's hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they're so different from anything else."

Roughly 25 years later, fresh evidence emerged when Willmott's colleague Andrés Orellana encountered a group of hungry Colobura caterpillars feeding on a young Cecropia tree in Venezuela.

The caterpillars were rapidly stripping leaves from the sapling. They possessed the familiar black body segments near the head and yellow spines characteristic of the genus, but one feature stood out.

Unlike the two recognized species, these caterpillars had no cream-colored markings at all.

Orellana photographed the unusual insects and shared the images with Willmott. The discovery provided a compelling reason to investigate whether a third species had been overlooked.

Sapkota had recently joined the Shirey lab at the Florida Museum and was eager to lead the investigation.

Working with her colleagues, she designed a study that combined genetic evidence with careful examinations of butterfly anatomy.

First, she studied DNA barcodes, short and highly variable genetic sequences that help researchers distinguish species. These sequences came from a long-running survey of butterflies and moths in Costa Rica led by study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs.

The investigation then expanded to older butterfly specimens collected across tropical Central and South America. Sapkota sent these museum samples to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, where researchers sequenced both their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

The genetic results provided a way to test whether the butterflies represented genuinely different evolutionary groups rather than ordinary variations within a single species.

But the researchers also wanted to know whether there were physical differences that previous scientists had failed to notice.

An Invisible Clue Hidden in Butterfly Wings

Sapkota spent hours examining preserved butterflies in museum collections, searching for consistent traits that might distinguish the suspected species.

At first, the effort produced few answers. Other than the slight differences in the gray wing stripe, the butterflies appeared remarkably similar.

Eventually, she noticed something unusual.

The undersides of some wings appeared to have a faint violet shimmer, and the intensity of that sheen seemed to vary between specimens.

This observation suggested that the insects might reflect ultraviolet light, which falls outside the range of human vision but can be detected by many butterflies.

"I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn't look violet to me, it reflected UV light," she said.

The measurements revealed a striking pattern. All three species reflected ultraviolet light, but the wavelengths differed.

The researchers named the newly identified species Colobura cryptica, reflecting its previously concealed identity.

Although the visible differences were extremely subtle, the ultraviolet measurements, caterpillar markings, and DNA results told a consistent story.

The three species could be distinguished by the following features:

There is an additional complication with Colobura dirce. It includes two subspecies with different ultraviolet reflectance values. Colobura dirce dirce reflects light at 362.2 nm, while Colobura dirce wolcotti reflects light at 390.6 nm. The 376 nm value represents the average for the species.

Beyond these minor wing differences, Sapkota could not identify any other consistent anatomical distinctions. Even the male genitalia, which often provide some of the most reliable features for separating butterfly and moth species, appeared indistinguishable.

Nevertheless, the genetic findings were decisive.

DNA analysis identified three distinct evolutionary lineages, and those divisions matched the physical differences the team had documented. Together, the evidence confirmed that Colobura contains three species rather than two.

Three Butterfly Species Living Side by Side

Identifying a previously unknown butterfly species is significant on its own, but the geographic distributions of these three species make the finding particularly intriguing.

All three occur in overlapping portions of Central and South America.

Colobura dirce has the widest distribution, extending from Mexico to southeastern Brazil. It occurs on both sides of the Andes Mountains and throughout the Caribbean archipelago.

Colobura annulata also occupies a large geographic area, although it is absent from the Greater Antilles.

The newly described Colobura cryptica has the smallest known range, stretching from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.

These overlapping distributions raise an important evolutionary question. How did three species become genetically distinct while continuing to occupy many of the same regions?

Species often emerge when populations become isolated from one another. A mountain range, for example, might divide a population and prevent individuals on opposite sides from mating.

Over many generations, the separated groups can accumulate different genetic and physical traits. If those differences become great enough, the populations may eventually lose the ability to interbreed, even if they come into contact again.

But geographic separation is not the only mechanism that can drive the formation of new species.

Researchers suspect that the Colobura butterflies might have developed different ways of using their shared forest habitats.

"There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies," Sapkota said. "Colobura dirce is typically found in the undergrowth and C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies."

In other words, one species may spend more time near the forest floor while the others favor the upper branches.

This kind of habitat separation could potentially help maintain differences between species living in the same geographic area.

However, previous research has produced inconsistent observations. One reason may be that even experienced butterfly specialists have difficulty telling the three species apart.

How Do Nearly Identical Butterflies Recognize Each Other?

An even more puzzling question concerns how the butterflies identify suitable mates.

Many moths and some butterflies use special scent glands to release pheromones, chemical signals that help individuals recognize members of their own species.

That suggests visual information may play an important role in mate selection. Yet their nearly identical appearance makes it difficult to understand how they distinguish one species from another.

The newly discovered ultraviolet differences offer a possible explanation.

Although humans cannot see ultraviolet light, many butterflies can. Sapkota suspects that the different ultraviolet reflections from their wings might provide visual signals that help them identify members of their own species.

Similar mechanisms are known or suspected in other butterflies and moths. Garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths possess ultraviolet-reflecting wing scales that researchers believe may contribute to mate selection.

Sapkota is investigating whether Colobura butterflies use comparable signals, but the results have not yet provided a clear answer.

Whatever mechanism they use, the butterflies appear remarkably successful at maintaining their separate identities.

Analysis of nuclear DNA found no evidence of hybridization among the three species, despite their overlapping ranges.

The findings suggest that the species have followed separate evolutionary paths without detectable genetic mixing.

A Familiar Butterfly Still Holds Many Secrets

The discovery of Colobura cryptica demonstrates how much remains unknown about even widespread, conspicuous animals.

For generations, naturalists studied these butterflies without recognizing the full diversity hidden within the group. Only by combining detailed observations with modern genetic testing and ultraviolet measurements were researchers able to uncover the third species.

Yet some of the most important questions remain unanswered, including how the butterflies choose mates, whether they occupy different parts of the forest, and what originally caused their evolutionary separation.

For Sapkota, answering those questions will require observing the insects in their natural habitats.

"Someone has to go the field to find it out themselves."

Those interested in another unusual aspect of Colobura biology can explore the Biodiversity Heritage Library, which contains a whimsical account published in 1952 describing the poop perches that young Colobura caterpillars construct during their earliest developmental stages.

Additional study co-authors include Andrés Orellana of the Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira; Nick Grishin and Leina Song of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Isidro Chacón of the Museo Nacional Santo Domingo de Heredia; Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs of the University of Pennsylvania; and Sajan KC of the Florida Museum of Natural History.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Welch Foundation, Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (NFRFt-2020- 00073), the Canada Foundation for Innovation's Major Science Infrastructure program (MSI 42450), BioAlfa, and Project UNET (Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira).

#725. 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space

It now takes 24 hours for even a single particle of light to reach Voyager.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe.

Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.

"The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance."

The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond.

On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn.

"Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries.

"And then, as Voyager 1 continued out to the Saturn system, it actually discovered that Saturn's large moon Titan has a very thick atmosphere surrounding it," she added. "So it's one of the only moons that has a thick atmosphere."

Decades later, Voyager 1's data is still incredibly important for scientists studying the planets and moons of our cosmic neighborhood. Phillips works on Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's ocean moon Europa. And the basis of that work stems from early observations by Voyager.

"Every time I get to use data from Voyager, I have to kind of think back to where that data came from," Phillips said. "I think about kind of the legacy, the missions that really set the precedent for a mission like Europa Clipper. Voyager is right there at the top of the list. And some of those images that we took with the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft of Europa — they're actually still, for some portions of Europa, they're the best pictures that we have. So, we're still using that data today, almost 50 years later."

Today, Voyager 1 and 2 are both exploring interstellar space. On Aug. 25, 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to leave the heliosphere, or the protective bubble of solar particles that surrounds the planets and other objects in our solar system. After crossing that boundary, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space and has been exploring the interstellar medium ever since. Voyager 2 followed suit in November 2018.

While the Voyager spacecraft have left the heliosphere, they have technically not left the solar system, as they are still within the gravitational influence of the sun. Today, Voyager 1 is traveling 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) through interstellar space, exploring farther than any human-made object in history.

The Voyager mission team communicates with Voyager in radio waves via the Deep Space Network, a collective of giant radio antennas that NASA uses to "talk" to a wide range of far-off spacecraft. And since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours for communications to reach Voyager 1, and then another 24 hours for any response to return.

"You need to have patience because now, if you send a command to Voyager, Voyager receives that command 24 hours later," Spilker said. "So two days later, you receive confirmation that yes, Voyager one received your command and is sending back the information that you'd like it to send back."

That patience is important, as the nearly-50-year-old Voyager mission is still actively making science observations and collecting new data. While some of the probes' science instruments have had to be shut off over the years to save battery life, both probes are still going strong.

"It is always difficult when an instrument has to get turned off, knowing that it has returned good science data for so many years," Spilker said. "But a plan was laid down to make sure we had at least one instrument operating on each spacecraft, one type of instrument, for as long as we could."

As long as the mission is active, the team will continue to investigate the unknown with Voyager. After all, ever since the probes entered interstellar space, they have been exploring areas of space that we've only ever studied remotely or in theory.

"Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, and what we knew about interstellar space at that point really came just from remote observations and theories. And so, right away, Voyager started to find that what we expected was not exactly right," Spilker said.

So far, the team has found that the sun's influence extends much farther from the heliopause than they expected. The Voyagers have observed and measured "ripples coming from the sun," as Spilker described them, deep in interstellar space.

"Voyager is going to continue to measure the cosmic rays and particles, and also the radio waves coming from interstellar space and coming from the sun," Spilker said, adding that the team is always eagerly "waiting to see if there might be more surprises out there."

How has this mission from the 1970s continued to not just survive but actively push forward through all of that time, overcoming countless hurdles and unexpected challenges?

"Voyager's longevity is really a tribute to all of the people who worked on Voyager, from those who designed the spacecraft, built it, programmed its computers, launched it, and then the teams of individuals that have flown it over that 50 years," Spilker said.

Spilker is a longtimeVoyager veteran. Fresh out of school, she started her NASA career with Voyager, working on the mission for about a decade before moving on to NASA's Cassini Saturn mission. After Cassini concluded with a dramatic death dive into Saturn in 2017, Spilker returned to Voyager, where she serves as a project scientist today.

"I'm very proud and happy to work on Voyager," she said.

The Voyager team is small, with just eight to 10 people on the flight team, according to Spilker. But they often bring in retired scientists and Voyager team members from decades past who are eager to share their knowledge and connect with the new generation of mission scientists and engineers.

"Voyager is multi-generational," Spilker shared. "We have someone whose parents weren't born when Voyager was launched, and then we just celebrated the 90th birthday of one of the members who retired and came back. He actually helped to build and program the computers on Voyager."

Looking to the future, the team is pressing on full speed ahead to continue science with Voyager. Another big milestone is just ahead, when the mission turns 50 this upcoming year. And Spilker is optimistic that this will not be the end.

"I see the 50th anniversary as just a milestone," Spilker said. "The next milestone, and then we'll just keep on going."

As Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, you might wonder whenVoyager 2 will hit the same milestone. Since Voyager 2 is on a slower trajectory,it won't reach one light-day from Earth until 2035, nearly a decade into the future. The Voyagers are both hardy and tough, so it's not crazy to think the probe may still be alive when it crosses that threshold.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #724. Prince Harry Shares How Archie, Lilibet Changed With U.K. School

Months after Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's kids Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet began classes, the Duke of Sussex shared how their new school has changed them.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's kids have been rather chuffed about their royal return to the United Kingdom.

More than two months after Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, began the school year, their dad shared insight into how they've adjusted to classes across the pond.

"They love being back," Harry explained on the Nov. 20 episode of This Morning, though with him and Meghan having lived in the United States since 2020, he clarified, "I say back—they never really knew."

Archie was born in London in 2019, leaving just a year later when his parents moved to the U.S.—where they were living when Lilibet arrived in 2021. For the kids, school has been a big way of acclimating to life in the U.K. And though that hasn't been without some hiccups, as they had to switch schools two days after classes began because of security concerns, they've reigned supreme through the ups and downs of life in a new country.

"It's a big culture shift," the Duke of Sussex explained. "The kids in school uniforms is a big change for them, but it's certainly helped. The confidence in both of them has gone through the roof since being at a U.K. school, which is really, really nice."

While they spent the first few years of their lives under the California sun, they're sounding more and more English every day. He quipped, "I'm squeezing the accents out of them. Their friends at school are doing the same."

"It's great being back on home soil," the 42-year-old said. "I'm throwing myself into the new winter weather, which is also nice. I missed that a bit."

#723. Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery

Deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

The discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.

Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.

A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils

One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals showed so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.

To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.

The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.

The researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.

To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.

Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?

Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.

"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins."

The results raise important questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.

Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.

However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.

Another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.

Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.

Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution

The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.

Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.

"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.

"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex."

The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.

Whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an important new perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.

As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.

#722. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

Crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent."

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#721. Germany gives sweeping powers to police, intelligence services

Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?

Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Germany's foreign intelligence service, will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.

Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Historian Sönke Neitzel of the University of Potsdam considers the separation principle understandable in its historical context. At the BKA's autumn conference, however, he described it as "nonsense" in light of today's threat landscape and said it was no longer necessary in a country that has been a constitutional democracy for decades.

While Neitzel considers the separation principle outdated, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU) wants to preserve it in its essential form. In his view, even a more extensive exchange of data does not violate the principle. At the same time, however, he has made clear that he wants to transform the domestically focused Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the BND into "real intelligence services."

This legislative reform brings Dobrindt a significant step closer to that goal. Parliament approved the interior minister's plans with the votes of the governing coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dobrindt insisted that Germany intends to take an active approach to defending itself against cyberattacks: "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back. They must know that their digital infrastructure, their server infrastructure, and their software will also be targeted by us."

BKA President Holger Münch welcomes Dobrindt's determination and points to the growing threat posed by cyberattacks. The line between criminal and state-sponsored actors is becoming increasingly blurred, he argues. As a result, both intelligence services and law enforcement agencies face the same challenge.

To underscore the scale of the threat as he sees it, Münch cited two statistics: in the first six months of 2026, crime originating from abroad rose by 24% compared with the same period the previous year. What concerns him most is that fewer than 5% of these cases are solved. The BKA chief considers this trend more dangerous than ever: "The state's promise of security can become fragile. Confidence in the ability of its institutions to act effectively and remain steadfast is declining."

This article was originally written in German.

#720. ‘Incredibly frustrating’: prestigious fellowship applications close in just 21 hours

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty

Swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship. On 14 November, he stayed up through the night completing the form and coordinating with referees across different time zones.

After sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking. When he returned to submit it at around 8.50 p.m., applications had closed. The fellowship had reached its limit of 800 applications within 21 hours of opening.

Chowbey is not alone. Many researchers around the world found themselves unable to submit applications last Sunday and took to social media to vent their annoyance.

“It is incredibly frustrating to invest so much time and effort into developing a strong scientific project, only to discover that the timing of the application process may put some researchers at a disadvantage — especially when you open the system on Sunday and close it the same day,” wrote Ida Skubis, an AI researcher at Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland, on the social-media platform LinkedIn.

The Humboldt Research Fellowships support researchers from abroad to conduct research in Germany, providing €3,000 (US$3,300) a month for postdoctoral researchers and €3,600 a month for experienced researchers. Fellowships can last for 6–24 months for postdocs and 6–18 months for experienced researchers.

The fellowships and awards are recognized internationally, which is why they are so competitive, says Marcela Hernández, an environmental microbiologist at the University of Birmingham, UK, and a former fellow. “Being a Humboldtian is a mark of academic distinction. It has an exceptional international network.”

A spokesperson for the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation in Bonn, Germany, said in a statement to Nature that it had not anticipated that the application cap would be reached within 24 hours of opening. The foundation introduced the cap this year because it has seen a large increase in applications since 2024. It holds application rounds in March, July and November.

The spokesperson said that as more researchers have used AI to help prepare their applications more quickly, the volume of applications has increased. Humboldt does not prohibit the use of generative AI in applications, nor are applicants required to declare AI use.

Simon Hammann, a chemist at the University of Hohenheim in Stuttgart, Germany, supported a research proposal as a prospectiveacademic host for someone who was able to submit their application successfully. He says that opening the call on a Sunday disadvantaged researchers with family and caring responsibilities. “That should definitely be changed.”

The Humboldt spokesperson said that the foundation advertises the date when applications will open, but that unfortunately the date fell on a Sunday this time.

“We recognize the impact this had on those who were unable to apply, particularly given the challenges of coordinating availability over a weekend. We sincerely apologize for the disappointment and frustration this has caused,” the spokesperson said.

They added: “We will take this as an opportunity to continue reflecting on and improving our processes” to “find a transparent and fair solution”.

Thermal satellites from an Indian startup aim to spot urban heat, crop stress and wildfires from orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time.

SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a "thermometer for Earth" in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence, the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says.

"It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview.

That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs.

The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches.

Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai.

"We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO.

First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology.

Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany.

The company has raised roughly $6 million since it was founded in 2023, and it holds letters of intent worth $54 million from prospective customers, Bakhai said.

SatLeo grew out of a government project that used satellite data for farming insights. Its founders found existing thermal data, such as from the U.S. government's Landsat satellites or Earth-observing craft operated by the San Francisco company Planet Labs, too coarse for India's fragmented farmlands, Bakhai said. When field teams and drones couldn't fill the gap at scale, "we realized space is the only solution," he said.

SatLeo's orbital ambitions take shape on the ground, inside a light-blocked cleanroom at the company's headquarters here in Ahmedabad. When Space.com visited in late October, about three weeks after TAPAS-1 launched, a handful of engineers in cleanroom coats were already fine-tuning its successor, TAPAS-2.

The payload itself sat perched on a solitary, nondescript table with a thick, hole-filled steel top meant to dampen vibrations from footsteps, traffic and the like. The room's only window was covered by a thick black blind to seal out stray light, a necessity for calibrating sensors meant to track the planet's thermal pulse from a few hundred kilometers up.

Despite its small size, the payload is built to collect enormous amounts of data. How much detail a payload can capture "all depends upon the architecture of the detector," said SatLeo co-founder Ranendu Ghosh, a former scientist at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

The design captures two infrared bands, mid-wave and long-wave, on the same payload. The company says this lets a single design serve both civilian and defense uses: long-wave suits applications like agriculture, while the hotter signatures of fires or missile launches show up better in mid-wave.

TAPAS-1 took just six months to build, and TAPAS-2 is on a similar timeline: It's expected to be ready by February 2027, according to the team.

Access to government test facilities explains much of that speed, Bhati said. Rather than buy capital-intensive equipment, such as a thermal vacuum chamber that mimics conditions in space, the company calibrates its payloads at facilities run by IN-SPACe, the government agency that supports private space firms, and ISRO's Space Applications Centre, both in Ahmedabad.

A small group of former ISRO scientists, about eight among a staff of around 40, also mentored the younger workforce and "really made this journey a little faster for us," Bakhai said.

Ghosh, who spent more than two decades at ISRO, said the nature of a private company helps, too. "When I was in ISRO, I saw people delivering this kind of a payload," he said. "I never saw it delivered in less than a year."

He credited the SatLeo team's "zeal to deliver in time," along with fewer administrative challenges than at ISRO, which he described as an organization where "you cannot bypass the hierarchy."

The harder constraint, the founders said, is not building satellites but finding rockets to carry them to space. TAPAS-1's launch slipped from a planned February liftoff to October for lack of a ride, Bakhai said.

SpaceX is reportedly not accepting new bookings until at least 2029. In addition, Skyroot Aerospace, which in July became the first Indian company to reach orbit, is still flying development missions meant to validate its Vikram-1 rocket before it begins full-scale commercial operations.

"There is a challenge right now in terms of availability of launch vehicles," Bakhai said. Once additional Indian rockets, such as those built by Skyroot and Agnikul, are flying regularly, "things will be much easier."

SatLeo is among more than 400 space startups that have emerged in India since the government opened the sector to private participation in 2020. Driven by this new wave of private enterprise, the country's space economy — currently valued at about $9 billion — is estimated to reach $40 billion over the next decade.

Asked what advice they would give newcomers entering the growing industry, SatLeo's three co-founders offered a unified message for success: start with the problem, then decide what to build.

"If you're solving a problem," Bhati said, "then people will bet on you."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#718. Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

For decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history. That long-standing assumption is now facing new scrutiny. Observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which is constructing the largest three-dimensional map of the Universe, suggest that dark energy's influence may have changed over billions of years. Although the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish a discovery, it has renewed interest in a fundamental question: Could dark energy evolve rather than remain constant?

Researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity. In a 2025 study published in Physical Review D, an international team led by Prof. Özgür Akarsu of ITU's Department of Physics investigated a mathematical possibility that previous researchers had largely overlooked. Their analysis revealed a surprising scenario in which the effective density of dark energy was negative during the Universe's early history before eventually becoming positive.

The research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. The team also collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, who previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Akarsu's group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University's Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, an internationally recognized center for theoretical physics.

An Overlooked Possibility in Einstein's Theory of Gravity

The discovery came from examining a part of an existing theory that had received relatively little attention. Rather than proposing an entirely new explanation for dark energy, the researchers revisited a framework known as teleparallel f(T) gravity.

Einstein's general theory of relativity explains gravity through the curvature of spacetime. Teleparallel gravity takes a different mathematical approach, describing gravity through a property called torsion. Scientists have spent years studying modified versions of this framework to investigate whether gravity itself might account for the Universe's accelerating expansion.

Earlier investigations of an exponential form of teleparallel gravity had concentrated on one particular set of mathematical solutions. This approach reflected a familiar assumption inherited from general relativity: dark energy should always have a positive density.

Akarsu and his colleagues decided to investigate what would happen if that restriction were removed. By considering a previously neglected branch of the theory, they uncovered a substantially different picture of how the Universe might have evolved.

Dark Energy May Have Switched From Negative to Positive

The team's calculations showed that two distinct cosmic histories could emerge even when the Universe contains the same amount of matter today.

One mathematical solution closely resembles the standard model of cosmology. The other predicts that effective dark energy had a negative density in the distant past. According to this second possibility, the density reached zero at approximately redshift 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, before becoming positive and remaining that way.

What makes the result particularly interesting is that the researchers did not need to introduce an additional adjustable parameter to produce this behavior. Instead, the determining factor is related to the Universe's present matter density, which selects the mathematical branch. As a result, the model retains the same six cosmological parameters used in the standard ΛCDM model.

The theory also avoids an important potential problem. Although it predicts behavior that differs from Einstein's gravity across enormous cosmic distances, its departures from general relativity become naturally suppressed in dense environments. This allows the alternative solution to remain compatible with the highly accurate measurements of gravity made throughout the Solar System.

A Possible Explanation for the Hubble Tension

The new findings build on years of research into whether dark energy could have changed sign during the Universe's history.

Akarsu and his collaborators previously developed a framework called the sign-switching ΛCDM (ΛsCDM) model. In this scenario, the cosmological constant changes from negative to positive several billion years after the Big Bang.

Previous analyses found that a change in the sign of dark energy's density could agree with DESI observations while potentially reducing several unresolved disagreements in cosmology. One of the most significant is the Hubble tension, the persistent discrepancy between different methods of measuring the Universe's present expansion rate.

However, an important question remained unanswered. What underlying physical process could cause dark energy to undergo such a reversal?

The latest research offers a possible mechanism. Instead of requiring scientists to prescribe a sign change as part of the model, the reversal arises naturally from the mathematical structure of the modified gravity theory.

Akarsu explained why investigating an overlooked solution proved so valuable.

"For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI's. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself."

DESI Observations Raise New Questions About Dark Energy

The theoretical findings have become especially relevant as astronomers gather increasingly detailed measurements of cosmic expansion.

DESI tracks the locations of millions of galaxies and quasars, allowing researchers to reconstruct how the Universe has expanded across billions of years. In March 2025, the DESI collaboration released findings based on its first three years of observations.

When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak gravitational lensing, the results strengthened earlier indications that dark energy might not behave like a fixed cosmological constant.

These findings do not yet establish that dark energy changes over time. The statistical significance depends on which observational datasets are combined, and the evidence remains below the threshold required to claim a definitive discovery. Nevertheless, the possibility has motivated scientists to investigate alternative descriptions of cosmic expansion.

DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. The complete dataset will provide an even more demanding test of whether the apparent changes in dark energy persist as measurements become more precise.

The timing is also noteworthy. The ITU-led team's research was initially submitted in October 2024, several months before DESI announced its March 2025 findings. The researchers have not yet tested their model against the complete DESI dataset, making that comparison an important next step.

Could the Universe's Accelerating Expansion Be Slowing?

The significance of the proposed model extends beyond its prediction that dark energy's density may have changed sign.

Because the alternative solution emerges from a specific theory of gravity, it makes predictions about both cosmic expansion and how gravity behaves across the Universe. These predictions give astronomers ways to investigate whether the proposed cosmic history is consistent with observations.

Measurements of how galaxies and larger structures form and grow will be particularly important. Researchers can also examine how gravity bends light and how the Universe's expansion has changed over time. Among the most useful observational tests are structure growth, redshift-space distortions, and weak gravitational lensing.

Although comprehensive testing remains necessary, the initial results offer reasons for further investigation.

In an extended version of the theory that includes a cosmological constant, the researchers found that the model could remain consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background while allowing the higher present-day expansion rates obtained from local measurements. This makes it a potentially useful approach to understanding the Hubble tension.

The extended model also permits another intriguing possibility: the acceleration of the Universe's expansion could have weakened or even stopped in the relatively recent cosmic past. Recent studies examining DESI observations have raised similar questions about whether cosmic acceleration has remained steady.

Importantly, neither the proposed dark energy reversal nor a recent slowdown in cosmic acceleration has been established as an observational fact. Both remain possibilities that must be tested against increasingly precise data.

Revisiting Gravity Could Reveal a Different Cosmic History

The research highlights how familiar scientific theories can contain possibilities that were missed because earlier investigations relied on restrictive assumptions.

In this case, allowing effective dark energy to have a negative density exposed an alternative evolutionary history within an already established mathematical framework. The researchers suggest that examining similarly overlooked solutions in other modified gravity theories could lead to additional insights.

Ultimately, the strength of the new explanation will depend on how well it reproduces the Universe astronomers actually observe. The full DESI dataset and other cosmological measurements will help determine whether this unusual version of cosmic history deserves a place alongside established explanations.

"We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension," said Prof. Özgür Akarsu.

#717. The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

In May 2024, an extraordinary solar storm sent brilliant auroras across skies in parts of the world where the northern and southern lights are rarely visible. But the spectacular displays were only the most obvious signs of an enormous disturbance unfolding in space around Earth. Deep within the planet's magnetosphere, the vast region controlled by its magnetic field, scientists were witnessing something they had never directly measured before.

The event began when a large sunspot unleashed several powerful solar eruptions in rapid succession. As enormous clouds of magnetized plasma raced through space, they combined before slamming into Earth's magnetosphere. The resulting storm produced the strongest magnetic disturbance ever measured in Earth's ring current, a vast region of electrically charged particles surrounding the planet.

For decades, researchers have debated where the particles that make up this ring current come from. Two major sources are known: the solar wind, which carries charged particles outward from the Sun, and Earth's ionosphere, an electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere. Both typically supply particles during geomagnetic storms, and some scientists expected the solar wind to remain an important contributor during an extreme event involving particularly dense solar wind.

Instead, the first direct measurements of ring current composition during a storm of this magnitude revealed something remarkable. Particles originating from the solar wind contributed very little, while those coming from Earth's own atmosphere dominated to an extent never previously observed.

Published in Science Advances, the findings suggest that Earth's atmosphere may play a much greater role in determining the severity of extreme geomagnetic storms than scientists previously recognized. Because the dominant ions from Earth are much heavier than the particles supplied by the solar wind, they may have strengthened the magnetic disturbance and caused the ring current to reach its greatest intensity unusually close to the planet.

The discovery also strengthens the case for a proposed Japanese satellite mission designed to investigate how atmospheric particles enter space and influence powerful geomagnetic storms.

How the May 2024 Solar Superstorm Disrupted Earth's Magnetic Field

On May 10 and 11, 2024, enormous clouds of charged solar particles struck Earth's magnetosphere, triggering one of the most powerful geomagnetic storms in decades. Known as the "Gannon storm" or "Mother's Day storm," the event pushed the SYM-H index, a measure of geomagnetic disturbance, to a minimum of −518 nanotesla. This represented the second-largest recorded disturbance since 1981. The previous storm of comparable strength occurred in November 2004.

Although the colorful auroras drew worldwide attention, the consequences of such storms can extend far beyond the night sky.

"Some super or extreme geomagnetic storms are not just impressive light shows -- they pose radiation risks to spacecraft, disturb GPS signals and communications, and cause power outages. Understanding how a geomagnetic storm develops is not only a scientific question, but also one with real-world consequences," said Naritoshi Kitamura, lead author and designated assistant professor from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

A major source of these magnetic disturbances is Earth's ring current. This enormous belt of energetic charged particles, primarily oxygen and hydrogen ions, slowly circulates around the planet thousands of kilometers above the equator.

As the ions move, they create an electrical current that generates its own magnetic field. That field partly opposes Earth's natural magnetic field, weakening the magnetic field measured at ground level. The resulting changes are among the key signals scientists use to track the strength of geomagnetic storms.

Japanese Satellite Reveals an Unexpected Source of Storm Particles

Scientists were able to investigate the May 2024 storm in unusual detail thanks to Japan's Arase satellite, which was launched in 2016 and is operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). The ERG (Arase) science center is jointly operated by the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS)/JAXA and the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research/Nagoya University.

Arase travels through the region of space where Earth's ring current forms. Its scientific instruments can measure both the mass and energy of individual ions, allowing researchers to determine the types of particles present during a storm.

By remarkable timing, the spacecraft passed through the ring current shortly after the May 2024 storm began and again as the disturbance approached its peak. These observations provided a rare opportunity to examine the composition of the ring current during an exceptionally powerful geomagnetic event.

"This is the first simultaneous observation of ring current ions and solar wind during a storm this large, and the data was clear -- approximately 85% of ions were oxygen from Earth's own ionosphere," Kitamura explained.

The overwhelming contribution from Earth's atmosphere was particularly surprising because the storm had been triggered by dense streams of material arriving from the Sun. Rather than supplying most of the ring current ions, the solar wind played a relatively minor role in the measured particle population.

The Arase measurements revealed another extraordinary feature of the storm. The magnetic field weakened dramatically in a region much closer to Earth than where similarly severe reductions had previously been documented.

"Near the peak of the storm, Arase detected a 40% decrease in magnetic field intensity at roughly 16,000 kilometers above Earth, and much closer to Earth than similar large decreases previously documented."

At the same time, the satellite detected a decline in the number of energetic electrons that normally circulate through this region of space.

Such an extreme weakening of the magnetic field can alter the paths followed by these electrons, causing them to drift away from their usual orbits. However, scientists have not yet determined whether the deformation of the magnetic field directly caused the observed electron loss. Further research will be needed to establish that connection.

Together, the observations provide new insight into how the ring current behaves during especially intense geomagnetic storms. They also suggest that the unusually large population of heavy ions originating from Earth's atmosphere may have helped produce the severe magnetic disturbance so close to the planet.

A New Clue to Predicting Dangerous Solar Storms

The findings could have important implications for space weather forecasting. Current models rely heavily on conditions in the solar wind to estimate how powerful an approaching geomagnetic storm might become.

However, the new measurements suggest that conditions within Earth's own upper atmosphere could also influence a storm's eventual intensity. Understanding how many atmospheric ions escape into the magnetosphere, and how they contribute to the ring current, may therefore be essential for making more reliable predictions.

The researchers believe that additional satellite observations could help answer these questions. Their findings support FACTORS, a proposed mission involving two satellites that is being prepared for an upcoming JAXA proposal opportunity.

FACTORS would investigate the processes that allow ions from Earth's atmosphere to flow into the magnetosphere and examine how those particles contribute to the development of geomagnetic storms.

By revealing how Earth's atmosphere and incoming solar material interact during extreme events, the mission could eventually improve forecasts of dangerous space weather. More accurate predictions would help scientists better anticipate storms capable of disrupting satellites, navigation systems, communications networks, and power infrastructure.

Materials provided by Nagoya University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#716. The Lego Star Trek bridge diorama set should be your gateway to finally watching the Original Series

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

The Lego Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise Bridge diorama is a wonderful bit of nostalgia and a stunning recreation of a sci-fi icon. The playset features arguably feel a little out of place, given that the audience for this set will be older fans who want to board the Starship Nostalgia. But maybe that's the whole point: Making old Trek more accessible to young 'uns.

Beautiful diorama recreating the iconic sci-fi set.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek.

Before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it.

But now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch.

And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the new Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets.

Let's start with the Band-Aid rip: this set is $200. I know; it stings, especially when Star Trek promised us a future where money doesn't exist. But at 1701 pieces (nice, I see what you did there), it's much better value from a bricks-per-dollar perspective than the X-Files set we checked out recently.

Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built.

As the name suggests, you get a full Lego-ified recreation of the bridge of the USS Enterprise (NCC-1701, no A, B, C, or D). This includes Captain Kirk's chair, the helm positions ahead of him (manned by Chekov and Sulu), and all of the surrounding computer displays where you usually find Spock, Uhura and Scotty.

There's even a viewscreen that can sit in front of the crew, displaying an adorable Klingon commander facing off against Kirk.

Board the legendary starship and meet the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 for an amazing building experience. Recreate the iconic bridge and transporter room that served as the backdrop for epic scenes from "Star Trek: The Original Series".

Alongside the main bridge, there are a few fun extras bolted on, including a rotating transporter pad (which can make minifigures "disappear") and a working turbolift door connected to the back of the main bridge diorama. You'll have to make the swoosh sound effect yourself, though.

It's a wonderfully faithful recreation of Kirk's command center, complete with computer panels and screens, swiveling chairs and that weird scope thing that Spock was always looking into.

That said, it's a little lacking in proper Easter eggs. There are some tribbles hiding around the build, and the monitors have custom stickers showing cool Trekkie things. The weapon display racks on the back hold an array of pointy Klingon blades, Starfleet phasers, Sulu's fencing rapier and even Spock's harp, but compared to, say, the X-Files set we built recently, it feels a bit lacking in those deep-cut references.

All in all, it's a fantastic little diorama, but when it was announced, I'll admit I was a little puzzled as to who it was aimed at. "Star Trek fans, duh!" is the obvious response, but the Venn diagram crossover between "people who are nostalgic for the original series of Star Trek" and "people who want to buy $200 Lego sets" has to be pretty small, right?

Star Trek first aired way back in 1966, which means the first generation of fans are now 70 years old and upwards. Lord knows I hope I'm still building Lego sets when I'm 70, but is that a large enough crowd to make this set a success? Then again the show was repeated and syndicated throughout the 70s and 80s, which means hopefully there'll be some younger buyers, too.

The playset aspects of the set are even more puzzling. The working door, exploding monitor and spinning transporter pad are great additions to a kids' playset, but this isn't that — it's a display for nostalgic Star Trek fans. The design of the set just feels a bit confused.

But then it hit me. Maybe this isn't just for fans of the original series; maybe it's meant to create some new fans. I started watching the original Star Trek 60 years after its debut because… well, I'm the sci-fi editor for a space website, and it felt wrong that I hadn't seen it. But most people don't have that sort of professional impetus. The average person won't jump back to watch a 60-year-old TV show without a polite nudge, and this set does a great job of highlighting the charm and optimism of Star Trek's debut outing.

I don't know, maybe I'm just projecting here. Maybe Lego bought the rights to make Star Trek sets and needed something to do after they'd mined all the nostalgia they could from the excellent Enterprise D set they released in 2025. Maybe this is just a toy for big kids.

Or maybe… just maybe, it's meant to inspire the next generation of Star Trek fans to check out where the magic started.

Disclaimer: We were sent a copy of the Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge set by Lego.

Ian is the Entertainment Editor at Space.com, covering movies, TV series, and games in the space and sci-fi realms. He's a massive sci-fi nerd and has been writing about games and entertainment for over eight years, with articles on sites like Space, LiveScience, GamesRadar, and more. With a degree in biology, a PhD in chemistry, and his previous role at the Institute of Physics Publishing, Ian is taking a world tour through the different scientific disciplines.
