#715. NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks

Organic carbon has been confirmed in two ancient Martian rocks examined by NASA's Perseverance rover, adding an important new piece to the puzzle of whether Mars once supported life. Even more surprising, the material was found just beneath the planet's surface, where harsh conditions can destroy organic compounds.

The discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature. A potential biosignature is a substance or feature that could have formed through biological activity, although other explanations are possible. Now, research published in Science Advances provides definitive confirmation that the same two rocks, located in Mars' Bright Angel formation, contain organic carbon, an essential component of life. The findings also offer a clearer picture of the material's characteristics and how it may have been preserved.

The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.

NASA's Perseverance Rover Detects Complex Organic Carbon

To investigate the rocks, researchers used the Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument mounted on Perseverance's robotic arm. The instrument examined several rocks in the Bright Angel formation within Jezero crater, where the rover also collected a sample from a rock named "Cheyava Falls."

SHERLOC uses a technique called Raman spectroscopy, which shines laser light onto a material to identify and map its minerals and organic compounds without damaging the rock.

The measurements revealed macromolecular carbon (MMC), a form of carbon consisting of large, interconnected networks of carbon atoms. This type of material is also found in rocks on Earth and in meteorites. Importantly, it can form through biological activity or through chemical processes that do not involve life, so its presence alone cannot establish that Mars was once inhabited.

The surrounding geology offers additional clues about how the material reached these rocks. Billions of years ago, water flowed through a river channel into Jezero crater, carrying sediment that gradually settled on the bottom. Over time, those fine particles hardened into the mudstone formations Perseverance is now exploring.

Researchers detected the carbon within these ancient sediments and alongside carbonate and sulfate minerals that developed later as water altered the rocks. This distribution raises the possibility that organic material entered or formed within the rocks during at least two separate periods of Mars' geological history.

"While the specific formation mechanism of the MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones remains unknown, this is still one of the most exciting findings to date," Murphy said.

Organic Carbon Survives Just Beneath Mars' Harsh Surface

One of the most striking results concerns where the organic carbon was found. The material survived only a few microns below the exposed Martian surface, at a depth smaller than the thickness of a sheet of paper. This is the shallowest detection of macromolecular carbon ever reported on Mars.

That location makes the finding particularly unusual. Mars' surface is exposed to radiation, sunlight, and chemically reactive substances that can break down organic molecules. Scientists would generally expect these conditions to make long-term preservation especially difficult so close to the surface.

"The Martian surface environment includes radiation and chemical oxidants that are destructive to organics, and terrestrial laboratory simulations have shown that the survival time of organics in Martian-like conditions -- especially at or near the surface -- depends on factors such as the type of organic molecule and the surrounding minerals," Murphy said. "The MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones is either resistant to degradation and/or has been sufficiently shielded by other minerals, such as clays, or iron-rich Martian soil."

In other words, the carbon may have survived because of its own chemical durability, protection provided by surrounding minerals, or a combination of the two. Understanding how it endured could help scientists determine where similar organic compounds might remain preserved elsewhere on Mars.

Ancient Martian Lakes and Rivers May Have Been Rich in Organic Material

The findings also suggest that organic carbon may not have been confined to a single region of ancient Mars.

Perseverance collected the Bright Angel sample more than 2,000 miles from Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover previously detected organic compounds. Finding organic material at such widely separated locations suggests that the chemistry associated with life's building blocks may once have been common across the Martian landscape.

"It is encouraging for Martian habitability," Murphy said. "This indicates that billions of years ago, organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient lakes and rivers on Mars."

The possibility of widespread organic material is significant because ancient Mars once had environments containing liquid water. If organic compounds were also broadly available, some of those lakes and rivers may have offered important chemical ingredients for life.

However, discovering those ingredients does not mean that living organisms were present. Organic carbon can be produced without biology, and scientists still need to determine exactly how the material in the Bright Angel rocks formed.

Could Martian Rocks Preserve Evidence of Ancient Life?

Determining whether the Bright Angel formation contains fossilized microorganisms remains beyond the capabilities of the rovers currently exploring Mars. Neither Curiosity in Gale Crater nor Perseverance in Jezero Crater carries the large, energy-intensive laboratory equipment needed to conclusively distinguish fossil evidence of ancient life from geological processes.

Perseverance was designed to search for potential biosignatures, including features like those identified in the Cheyava Falls rock. From that perspective, the discovery represents a "resounding win for Mars science," Murphy said.

The next major step would be to examine Martian samples using the more sophisticated instruments available in laboratories on Earth. Such equipment could reveal details too small or chemically subtle for the rover's instruments to resolve, helping researchers determine whether biological processes or nonliving chemistry produced the organic carbon.

If samples from the Bright Angel formation eventually reach Earth, scientists hope to study their minerals and organic compounds with much greater sensitivity and resolution. These investigations could help explain how the macromolecular carbon formed, how it survived, and what its presence reveals about the distribution of organic material across Mars.

Murphy continues to collaborate with the SHERLOC science team as Perseverance explores the Martian surface. Her research also includes studying Earth materials that resemble Martian rocks and using Raman spectroscopy to improve how scientists interpret the measurements returned by the rover.

Murphy's work on SHERLOC Instrument Mars 2020 was supported through JPL Subcontract No. 1641753 to the Planetary Science Institute.

Materials provided by Science Advances. Original written by Mikayla Mace Kelley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#714. Every Track From ‘Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album’ Ranked

GTA's accompanying soundtrack arrived 24 hours after the long-anticipated Rockstar video game.

Monocultural moments in society have become extremely rare in the mid-2020s, but the arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI has brought about as strong a unified pop-culture tidal wave as we’ve seen this decade.

Rockstar Games released the Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album on Friday (Nov. 20) through Atlantic Records as an accompanying soundtrack to the long-awaited video game, which arrived 24 hours earlier.

Rockstar didn’t spare any expense when piecing together the 34-track album, which features Playboi Carti, Dua Lipa, Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, Gunna, Don Toliver, Kodak Black, Yung Lean, Future, Metro Boomin, Travis Scott, Fred again.., PinkPantheress, Morgan Wallen, Tame Impala, Fuerza Regida and more.

GTA VI will look to make even more history with a No. 1 debut on the charts — as no video game soundtrack has topped the Billboard 200 before.

Artist-hosted radio stations dominate the Vice City airwaves, with stations helmed or curated by the likes of Bad Bunny, Lana Del Rey, Morgan Wallen, Trina and Trick Daddy, PinkPantheress, Burna Boy and Robyn.

The Grand Theft Auto VI festivities will continue into the weekend, with a music festival at Miami’s Mana Wynwood on Nov. 21. The festival is set to have Cardi B, Travis Scott, Rauw Alejandro and more hit the stage, including a Cactus Jack ensemble featuring Scott, Don Toliver, SoFaygo and a cameo from Florida’s own Kodak Black.

Take a break from perusing Leonida with Jason and Lucia and find all 34 tracks from Grand Theft Auto: The Album ranked in order below.

Who knew Omar Apollo had a funky little party-starter like this up his sleeve? Drawing on the iconic Stalag riddim immortalized by Sister Nancy’s “Bam Bam,” “No Me Busques” bursts with a wailing chorus with an infectious call-and-response hook. Oh, and that festive saxophone riff. Lyrically, there’s not much to it beyond Apollo’s repeated insistence that someone stop looking for him. The groove does most of the talking. — ISABELA RAYGOZA

This track is a little different from what I’m used to, but I like it. It plays during the opening credits of GTA VI and serves as the opening track on the game’s album. Sonically, it has a heavy ’80s-inspired synth pulse, electro-disco drums and electric piano that make me feel like it could fit perfectly into any season of Stranger Things.

It’s the perfect way to open the game’s soundtrack. The song is about starting from zero and hustling your way toward success, which feels right at home in the world of GTA. It sets the tone for the kind of journey players are about to embark on. — CHRISTOPHER CLAXTON

Primal percussion, glitchy electronics and unbridled sexual energy collide on Arca’s self-produced “Sandunguea.” The Venezuelan experimentalist delivers a delirious invitation to dance and indulge, peppering her verses with colorful slang from her homeland. Against abrasive beats, her vocals switch between flirtation and feverish demands, breathy moans and fragmented chants. “Nuestra pasarela es la calle” (the street is our runway), she declares. In true Arca fashion, the dance floor becomes a space for uninhibited self-expression, where pleasure and chaos go hand in hand. — I.R.

“All Again” is about missing someone after a relationship has ended, and wondering whether the love, memories and heartbreak were worth it in the end. It captures that feeling of looking back on a relationship and questioning whether you’d put yourself through it all over again. I’m not sure I would. Would you? — C.C.

Rina Sawayama made waves with her assist on Charli xcx’s “Beg for You” in 2022, and the Japanese pop artist/model is back in the mainstream with the brooding “TRDWFE.” I’m going to be hearing Sawayama asking us to “submit” repeatedly when my head hits the pillow tonight — although “TRDWFE” sounds like it was tailor-made more for the likes of HBO’s The Idol than the GTA vibe. — MICHAEL SAPONARA

Metro is back on production for this one. It’s a quick track about flexing, so you already know the deal: money, cars, clothes and relationships. Thug keeps it short and straight to the point, delivering the kind of flex-heavy record that fits right into the GTA lifestyle. Just remember, anything born out of a criminal lifestyle comes with real consequences. — C.C.

Fcukers is back. The NYC duo’s first release since Ö comes with the house-leaning “Only One” and they’re here to start the party and blow out your speakers. If there’s a rave somewhere in Leonida, Fcukers is headlining. Can we get Tinashe to sprinkle her Popstar magic on a remix? Vocalist Shanny Wise even moonlights as a co-host of GTA Radio’s Stockyard FM alongside PinkPantheress and The Dare in the video game. — M.S.

All the baddies to the front, please! “GMA” stands for “Get Money Anthem,” because if you can’t make money in GTA, what the hell can you do? Hope y’all caught that reference. This is an upbeat party anthem celebrating women who make their own money, no matter how they earn it. JT isn’t knocking anybody’s hustle, and at this point, neither am I. Whether you’re stacking cash in the game or in real life, the message is to stay focused on your goals and tune out the criticism. Shoutout to all the ladies working traditional 9-to-5s, earning college degrees, dancing or hustling on the side. We see you! — C.C.

Keith Richards puts his own spin on Jimmy Reed’s 1961 blues classic “Bright Lights, Big City” for Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album. His version takes a different approach from Reed’s original, but Keith sounds right at home here. It’s a fresh take on a blues classic, and one that fits perfectly into the world of GTA. — C.C.

With GTA returning to Vice City, having Kodak Black involved was a must. He’s even a character playing himself in the video game’s campaign. A Yak and Don Toliver collaboration seems like an odd pairing on its face — then you mix in the chaotic skittering production, and both the artists and listeners are playing catch-up for the duration of “Let’s Rock.” — M.S.

Tee Grizzley is not one to mess with. “IKYFL” is an unapologetic statement about loyalty, street credibility, success and refusing to let anyone question how far he’s come. The track captures Tee’s mentality of protecting his circle, enjoying the rewards of his success and staying ready for anyone who tries to challenge him. This is one of those tracks that makes you feel untouchable when you’re cruising through Vice City. — C.C.

Tove Lo wasn’t a name I expected to see on the tracklist for GTA VI, but she makes it work and shuts down any detractors who didn’t think she’d belong. “Blood in Your Eyes” is the blaring experimental pop that should be pumping the dance floor at Leonida’s version of the Space and E11EVEN nightclubs in the game. — M.S.

Morgan Wallen colors outside the lines of country while leaning on his pop and R&B influences for “Last Thing You Need.” It’s a smooth, laid-back track for fans to throw on for a late-night cruise through the swamp lands of GTA‘s Leonida. — M.S.

Just when you think you’ve settled into the sleek reggaetón groove of “X,” JHAYCO throws a dance-floor curveball. Co-produced by the Puerto Rican star alongside Tainy and COZY, the track finds Jhay assuring a love interest that he’s nothing like her ex, dishing out a stream of suggestive compliments. But the real thrill comes during the bridge, when bright synths and a pulsating electronic beat give way to a euphoric break before the dembow kicks back in. It’s a catchy little club banger that doubles as a reminder of Jhay’s knack for melding reggaetón with EDM. — I.R.

Of course, the GTA team got the legend Robert Glasper to help close out the album! Bringing together bassist Stanley Clarke, drummer Yussef Dayes and pianist Robert Glasper, this track is straight vibes. No lyrics needed, just let the musicians do their thing. Named after Miami’s historic Overtown neighborhood, the track connects the game’s Vice City map to the real-world roots of Miami. A smooth way to bring the album home. — C.C.

Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album wouldn’t be complete without an Afro-fusion track like this. I love the simple, chant-like hook. This might become my new go-to morning affirmation before heading to work or starting a session in GTA. It’s an uplifting song about resilience, bouncing back from setbacks and continuing to reach for greater heights no matter who or what tries to hold you back.

This is the perfect song to play after a mission doesn’t go as planned. Burna is reminding us that no matter the setback or how people treat you, you’re still unstoppable. Nobody is better than you, so keep pushing and get “bigger, bigger, bigger, bigger, hey!” — C.C.

This is baby-making music. Dâm-Funk and The Time’s Jesse Johnson supply the groovy, funky vibes that have been a staple of the GTA series for over two decades. I’m glad the soundtrack composers made room for them here, because Gen Z isn’t going to know what hit them when a new generation of gamers presses play. — M.S.

JENNIE is taking another “Power Trip” with this dance-pop track. In JENNIE’s city, there are no limits. This is a celebration of confidence, status and the freedom to do whatever you want without worrying about who approves. She embraces a larger-than-life persona, putting herself at the center of attention while making it clear that she knows her worth. But there’s nothing wrong with a little self-love, so is this really a power trip? — C.C.

If you see Future and Metro Boomin on a track, nine times out of 10, it’s going to be a banger, and this song proves just that. Shoutout to Yung Lean, because I like the track, but I’m not entirely sure if his presence fits. We have Metro handling the production, of course, and Future’s trap-influenced sound just works perfectly over Metro’s production. The two have such a natural chemistry, and this track is another example of why their collaborations rarely miss.– C.C.

Zara Larsson is chasing carefree desire with “Fast Emotion,” and she has no shame about it. She just wants you to “make it reckless, leave [her] breathless, make [her] heart race.” This track is bright, upbeat and full of energy, making it perfect for cruising down Vice City. “Fast Emotion” is all about craving an intense, spontaneous connection and allowing yourself to get swept up in the excitement of the moment. Through imagery of summer nights, physical attraction and speed, Zara captures a romance that feels exhilarating. — C.C.

Outside of Drake, no rapper made more of 2026 than Don Toliver. “TF?” provides the gloomy soundscape where Toliver is at home, compared to “Let’s Rock.” The raunchy tune could’ve been left on the cutting room floor during his OCTANE sessions, but is a worthy addition to the GTA album. — M.S.

A Cherokee loaded with contraband, police sirens blaring and a desperate escape through the city — “Macacoa 2000” opens like a scene straight out of Grand Theft Auto. Over hard-hitting reggaetón produced by Dímelo Ninow, reminiscent of the genre’s gritty 2000s heyday, Rauw Alejandro narrates a chaotic cop chase in a rapid-fire flow. Near the end, the track switches gears into sultrier territory, with the silky R&B vocals that marked his breakthrough. But beneath the bravado is a deeper reverence for reggaetón’s roots. At the beginning, he salutes the genre’s pioneers and reflects on his own longevity: “Se trata de trascender en la música” (It’s about transcending through music). — I.R.

Lana Del Rey shines as Delta Dawne in her role as a co-host of the rebellious Back Country Radio station in GTA. It’s only right she also delivered on the soundtrack, as LDR revels in a tragic romance for her “Crazy for You” ballad. Enter a Jason and Lucia romance scene from the campaign, with Lana providing the accompaniment. — M.S.

Fuerza Regida trades corridos for a breezy reggaetón groove on “Suzuki,” a flirtatious, raunchy cut that finds the San Bernardino hitmakers venturing into new territory. Produced by Synthetic, the track glides on glossy electronic textures and a laid-back dembow bounce, while frontman Jesús Ortiz Paz delivers a string of shameless come-ons. From pole dancing and risqué fantasies to a cheeky reference to tusi (a.k.a. pink cocaine), the lyrics leave little to the imagination. The beat may be easygoing, but JOP clearly has no intention of behaving himself. — I.R.

If half of Camila Cabello’s heart is in Havana, the other half lies in Miami. The dulcet “Sweet Like Candy” is a solid effort from CC — and like a good piece of candy, it’s not too heavy or sour, as the Fifth Harmony solo star sticks the landing with a fun, surface-level pop song. It also makes me think about where she has been in the last two years, with Cabello largely out of the pop scene since 2024’s C,XOXO. Time for a comeback, Camila. — M.S.

“Everybody getting’ loose!” Produced by Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, Travis definitely found his pocket on this one. I can see this track growing in popularity over time, and it’s already one of my favorites on the album. You have to crank the volume all the way up for this one. There’s so much electronic-infused chaos packed into the production, making it feel like hip-hop built for the club. It fits flawlessly into the GTA universe. — C.C.

Gunna turned back the clock to the days long before he was running 5Ks and flexed a six-pack as a gym rat. The Atlanta native reunites with frequent collaborator Turbo on the production side for a hard-hitting trap banger that boasts a flow that will sound familiar to early Gunna fans from the days of his Drip or Drown and Drip Season series, when he was still rising through the rap ranks. — M.S.

For all the tenderness with which Kali Uchis and Helado Negro sing to each other, their message couldn’t be more blunt: lárgate (or “f–k off”). The Colombian American singer and Ecuadorian American musician explore the emotional contradictions of a relationship that’s run its course, alternating between wistful reflections and outright dismissal. The sweetness of their vocal interplay almost belies the bitterness of their words. — I.R.

Cardi B will always pop her s—t, and “Don’t Chart” is no different. From the Bronx all the way to Vice City, Cardi is talking her talk! The track marks her second release of 2026, following the arrival of “AH HA” in July. This is Cardi through and through: she’s “still poppin’, still winnin’, [and] you still hatin’.” The bouncy production is packed with flex after flex, touching on confidence, wealth, chart success and designer labels. Thank you, Cardi, for another boastful tongue-in-cheek anthem. — C.C.

I imagine Playboi Carti has thousands of songs in a folder on hard drives that he could lend out when needed. Whether it was Carti himself or right-hand producer F1LTHY, they made the right choice going with “Ahh Yea.” For Carti’s standards, “Ahh Yea” leans more into the poppier side of his artistry, and could easily be seen playing on the GTA radio while gamers cruise around Leonida. “Ahh Yea” seems like a holdover from the MUSIC era, and I wish we got more loosies like this from King Vamp. — M.S.

Argentine duo CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso bring their irreverence to the dance floor on “Sexy Magic,” a bouncy, seductive electronic collaboration with British pop artist PinkPantheress, producer Fred again.. and French house veteran Étienne de Crécy. Riding a groovy bassline and shimmering synths, the track pairs Paco’s playful Spanish delivery with PinkPantheress’ breathy English vocals. Psychedelic around the edges and funky at its core, “Sexy Magic” sounds tailor-made for a neon-lit night cruising through Vice City. — I.R.

New York is in the building! That opening line in the first verse, “You look prettier in person,” hits in this social media era. We all know what it’s like to meet someone in person after finding them online and being happy that they actually look like their pictures — or, in this case, look even better. Boogie, you did your thing with this one, my boy. This is about to go platinum in the crib: “I don’t wanna fight, I wanna dance tonight” — a perfect track for a late-night drive through Vice City.— C.C.

Dua Lipa has proven to be the queen of a soundtrack when she dished out the top 10 Hot 100 bop “Dance the Night” for Barbie in 2023. With an intro that seems to draw from Phil Collins’ “Don’t Lose My Number” and later interpolates KISS’ “I Was Made for Lovin’ You,” the pop star has a penchant for taking songs of yesteryear and making them digestible for today’s audiences. “Go Easy” is no different for the hitmaker, as Dua clears the decks and gears up to launch a new era in the first quarter of ’27. — M.S.

“Flower in a Hurricane” is the preeminent song from GTA VI. In a short time, it’s already essentially become the video game’s theme song, providing the soundtrack to key scenes, clips and compilations going viral on social media. Justice meshes its EDM roots with King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard’s rock while SZA and Kevin Parker join forces to sing about surviving the storm to make it out alive on the other side. It perfectly balances the angst of everything falling apart at any moment on the journey to Vice City glory. — M.S.

A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth.

Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf.

During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion.

Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter.

This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place.

Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres.

ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system.

But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova.

Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #712. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.

Justice scores its best-ever placing with GTA VI hit "Flower in a Hurricane."

Jamie Miller is No. 1 for a fifth week on the U.K.’s Official Singles Chart with breakthrough single “Babydoll” on the list published Nov. 20.

The Cardiff-born singer first hit the top spot in October, becoming the first male Welsh solo act to hit the summit of the charts since Shakin’ Stevens in 1984. “Babydoll” is currently up to No. 37 on the Billboard Hot 100, a new peak.

Speaking to Billboard in a recent Chartbreaker story, Miller commented on the song’s rapid rise. “It became this kind of phenomenon on TikTok,” he said of the track. “It feels like the song has kind of unified people, and it’s been so amazing to see how fun it’s been for everybody — from kids in Africa and people in Sweden to these amazing dance groups in America and TV shows in the U.K.”

Ashe’s “Stop the Wedding!” comes in at No. 2 and is a non-mover in the spot, her best-ever placing on the charts. Sombr’s “My Body Isn’t Ready” lifts two places to No. 3, and comes in the same week he was announced for a major slot at 2027’s Glastonbury Festival.

Tate McRae’s “Housewife” closes at No. 4, followed by Sienna Spiro’s previous chart-topper “Great Expectation” (No. 5).

#710. Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains

Why do some volcanoes send towering fountains of lava into the sky while others release molten rock in much calmer eruptions? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain these striking differences.

An international research team led by The University of Manchester investigated volcanic material from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma, Spain. Their findings reveal that a process known as "superheating" can dramatically slow the formation of crystals inside magma as it travels upward toward Earth's surface.

Superheating occurs when magma reaches temperatures above those at which its crystals would normally remain stable. The researchers found that this extra heat can keep magma relatively fluid for much longer than expected, potentially allowing it to rise rapidly and produce spectacular lava fountains.

The discovery, published in Nature Communications, offers new insight into a long-standing question in volcanology: How does magma's temperature history influence the way a volcano erupts?

How Extreme Heat Changes Magma Deep Inside Volcanoes

Magma is a mixture of molten rock, gases, and sometimes solid crystals beneath Earth's surface. Once it emerges from a volcano, it is called lava. Although temperature and chemical composition are important in determining how magma behaves, the new research suggests that the heating it experienced before an eruption can also make a major difference.

Under normal conditions, crystals begin forming as magma cools. This process often starts around tiny existing crystals that act as "seeds," providing surfaces on which additional crystals can grow.

Superheating can disrupt this process in two important ways. First, sufficiently high temperatures can dissolve the microscopic crystal seeds that would otherwise encourage new crystals to develop. Second, the heat changes the internal structure of the molten material, making it more uniform and less favorable for new crystal formation.

These changes matter because crystals affect magma's viscosity, which describes how easily a substance flows. As more crystals develop, magma generally becomes thicker and more resistant to movement. This can influence both its speed of ascent and the way trapped volcanic gases escape.

Lead author Dr. Barbara Bonechi, Research Associate at The University of Manchester, explained:

"The history of crystal and bubble growth can dramatically control how a magma erupts, in particular as more crystals grow, they eventually have a dramatic effect on magma viscosity. Until now, we did not fully understand the dynamics of crystal growth for magmas that received an injection of superheat just before ascent. But using our exciting and newly developed X-ray transparent pressure vessel combined with synchrotron X-ray microtomography, we can actually observe these processes 'in situ'."

Scientists Discover an Eight-Hour Delay in Crystal Formation

To investigate what happens inside superheated magma, the researchers recreated volcanic conditions in the laboratory using material collected from the Tajogaite eruption. The magma involved in that eruption may have experienced superheating before reaching the surface and while rising through Earth's crust.

The team conducted experiments under carefully controlled temperatures and pressures designed to reproduce conditions encountered by magma underground.

At Diamond Light Source, a major scientific research facility, the researchers used synchrotron X-ray microtomography to watch crystals develop in real time. This advanced imaging technique uses extremely powerful X-rays to examine the internal structure of materials in three dimensions without having to cut them open.

A specially developed pressure vessel that allows X-rays to pass through it made these observations possible while the magma was subjected to volcanic conditions.

The team also performed complementary experiments in Prague, where samples could be examined over longer periods outside the real-time imaging setup. Together, these approaches allowed the researchers to observe how different heating conditions affected the timing of crystal formation.

The results revealed a remarkable difference.

Magma that had not undergone superheating began producing crystals after approximately 20 minutes. However, when magma was subjected to strong superheating, the beginning of crystallization was delayed for more than eight hours.

This substantial delay suggests that intense heating can leave magma without newly forming crystals for far longer than scientists might otherwise expect, with potentially important consequences for volcanic eruptions.

Why Superheated Magma Could Produce Towering Lava Fountains

The researchers next explored how these laboratory findings might affect real volcanoes.

They incorporated the measured delays in crystal formation into computer models that simulate how magma rises through Earth's crust. These models account for changes in magma properties as the molten material moves toward the surface.

The simulations revealed two very different possibilities.

When superheating delays crystallization, magma can remain relatively fluid as it rises. Because it encounters less resistance to flowing, it may travel upward more rapidly, potentially creating conditions that favor dramatic lava fountains.

These spectacular eruptions occur when escaping volcanic gases propel molten rock high above a vent, producing jets and fountains of glowing lava.

In contrast, magma that begins crystallizing earlier becomes more viscous and tends to ascend more slowly. This slower movement gives volcanic gases additional time to escape, favoring gentler eruptions in which lava flows out onto the surface rather than being thrown high into the air.

Such behavior is known as an effusive eruption, a type of volcanic activity characterized primarily by flowing lava.

The findings suggest that even when volcanic systems have similar characteristics, differences in their earlier heating histories may help explain why their eruptions look and behave so differently.

A New Clue for Predicting Volcanic Eruptions

Understanding what happens to magma before it reaches the surface is essential for assessing volcanic hazards. Scientists monitor signals such as earthquakes, ground deformation, and volcanic gas emissions to identify changes within active volcanoes.

However, predicting exactly how an eruption will unfold remains difficult. Two volcanoes with seemingly similar magma compositions and gas conditions can still display markedly different eruptive behavior.

The new research suggests that the effects of superheating and the timing of crystal formation deserve greater attention in volcanic forecasting models.

By accounting for these previously underappreciated processes, researchers may eventually be able to better interpret volcanic monitoring data and assess whether rising magma is more likely to produce vigorous lava fountains or gentler lava flows.

The results do not mean that magma temperature alone determines how explosive an eruption will be. Instead, they identify another important piece of the complex physical processes that shape volcanic activity.

Co-author Dr. Margherita Polacci, Senior Lecturer in Volcanology at The University of Manchester, highlighted the potential importance of the findings for understanding volcanic hazards:

"Current volcanic hazard models typically focus on magma chemistry, gas content and pressure changes. This work suggests that pre-eruptive thermal history and crystallization kinetics may also play an important role in controlling magma ascent and eruptive behavior, with implications for volcanic hazard assessment."

Materials provided by University of Manchester. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The exceptional sci-fi movie, based on Andy Weir's book, stars Ryan Gosling as Ryland Grace, a middle-school science teacher who becomes key to saving the world. Together with Rocky, an alien he meets along the way, Grace must solve the riddle of the mysterious substance that's causing the sun (and Rocky's star) to die out.

Dec. 11 is a smart choice by MGM too, as it puts the sci-fi spectacle back in front of audiences a week ahead of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part 3. That's not a battle you want to get in the middle of.

If you missed "Project Hail Mary" in theaters the first time, I'd definitely recommend you try to catch one of these screenings. It's a beautiful movie — visually and emotionally — and it deserves to be seen on the big screen.

If you're not feeling up to a trip to the theaters, you can also catch "Project Hail Mary" from the comfort of your own home, as it's also streaming on Amazon Prime Video.

#707. What's going on with the polar vortex?

Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

#706. Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

Physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits. Using a new type of slow-motion electron camera, researchers were able to watch these incredibly fast movements in graphene, revealing how powerful electric fields can drive electrons between different energy states.

The effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor. Although this sounds impossible in everyday life, electrons can make comparable jumps in the quantum world.

These unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Physicists have long suspected that they could become increasingly important in high-speed semiconductor electronics, but observing exactly how they unfold has been a major challenge.

Now, researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich have directly tracked these transitions in graphene, a material made from an extremely thin layer of carbon atoms. Their findings, published in Nature, provide a detailed look at how electrons respond to intense electric fields generated by light.

How Electrons Cross Forbidden Energy Gaps

In semiconductors and similar materials, electrons are restricted to particular ranges of energy called energy bands. Between these bands are regions known as forbidden energy gaps, where electrons cannot ordinarily occupy stable states.

Under normal conditions, electrons tend to remain within their existing energy bands. However, the researchers observed something very different when they exposed graphene to intense pulses of light. The electric field accelerated the electrons and caused some of them to switch from one energy band to another, crossing the intervening gap through a quantum mechanical transition.

To capture these movements, the scientists developed an experimental technique that combines advanced laser technology with electron microscopy. This allowed them to examine electron behavior on timescales far too short for conventional imaging methods.

A Slow-Motion Camera Reveals Quantum Jumps

"If you want to know who has won a race, you have to watch all participants," explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. "Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving."

The key instrument is a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing an enlarged picture of a material's surface, as a traditional microscope would, it measures the energies of electrons and how they are moving. Researchers then use this information to create detailed maps showing how electrons are distributed across different energy states.

One of the biggest technical obstacles was combining these measurements with powerful light fields that oscillate at extremely high speeds. The team needed to drive the electrons into motion while simultaneously recording how their energies and movements changed.

"Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time," says Rupert Huber.

Ulrich Höfer, a collaborator on the project and a pioneer in ultrafast electron spectroscopy, describes the excitement of witnessing the effect firsthand.

"Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us - it was also made possible by the samples we used."

Ultra-Pure Graphene Makes the Discovery Possible

The experiment depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples manufactured at Forschungszentrum Jülich. These specially prepared carbon layers were only one atom thick and had to be nearly flawless for the measurements to work.

"These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another important factor for the study was the use of "rotated" graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly," emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

The carefully engineered material made it possible to distinguish the delicate quantum effects from interference caused by imperfections in the graphene.

What the researchers saw was remarkable. When exposed to sufficiently strong light fields, electrons crossed the forbidden energy gap with a transition probability reaching 100 percent.

This result highlights one of the most surprising features of Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Electrons can move between energy states with very high probability even when those states are separated by a substantial energy gap.

The crucial factor is how quickly the electrons approach the gap under the influence of the electric field. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which particles pass through a barrier in physical space.

A New Path Toward Light-Controlled Electronics

Beyond revealing a fundamental quantum phenomenon, the new imaging technique could help scientists understand what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled and predictable way.

The graphene experiments have already provided an important clue. Although the electrons initially move in an orderly fashion, their interactions with the material's crystal lattice gradually disrupt that motion. Understanding these effects could help researchers develop more precise ways to control electron behavior.

This knowledge is particularly valuable for future electronic technologies that could use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to direct electrons instead of relying entirely on electrical voltages. Such approaches could open new possibilities for manipulating electronic properties at exceptionally high speeds.

The researchers also expect their method to work with many other quantum materials, allowing scientists to investigate previously inaccessible electron dynamics and potentially discover new ways to control them.

As Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg explains, the achievement marks the beginning of a much broader exploration.

"Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely new possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light."

#705. Executive Turntable: Melissa Victor-Burkhardt Joins HYBE Global Label Services

Plus, Kristina Heney and Greg Lombardo join Pophouse, Prescription Songs promotes Caitlin Lopilato and more music industry hires and promotions.

HYBE has appointed Melissa Victor-Burkhardt as executive vp of global artist services for HYBE Global Label Services. Within the newly created role, Victor-Burkhardt will work with the company’s worldwide teams to help with project management. She will also oversee a team of project managers for marketing, commerce, distribution, DSP and streaming.

Victor-Burkhardt previously served as senior vp, head of publicity and brand strategy at Epic Records, where she worked with clients including Future, Travis Scott, 21 Savage, Giveon, Mariah The Scientist, Madison Beer and Zara Larsson. She has also worked at labels including Interscope, J Records/Jive Records, Virgin, Island Def Jam and Bad Boy Records.

“Melissa is a deeply experienced executive in the music industry who has worked across countless campaigns for global artists and has an acute understanding of the scope and teamwork required across both internal and external partners for demonstrated success,” Juan S. Arenas, president for HGLS, said in a statement. “She will work closely with our worldwide teams to strengthen and build an ecosystem that encourages services to HYBE IP, a continued collaborative approach, and a focus on high impact. I’m grateful to have her on board to help execute the vision of a globally built platform powered by best-in-class services.”

Victor-Burkhardt added, “By helping artists grow from a first single to the global stage, my work has always been about strategically building careers that last. HYBE is redefining what a music company can be, and I’m excited to bring that experience to a global platform. Thank you to Isaac Lee [CEO, HYBE Americas] and Juan S. Arenas for this opportunity.”

See more music industry signings and promotions below.

Pophouse has appointed Kristina Heney and Greg Lombardo to the company’s leadership team. Heney has been named president, commercial and marketing, and is based in New York, while Lombardo is president, Pophouse Avatar Network, and is based in Los Angeles. Heney joins from Oak View Group, where she had served as executive vp, marketing, media and conferences. Lobardo had been vp and global head of experiences at Netflix.

“Pophouse was founded on the belief that the world’s most iconic artists can reach new generations through bold, imaginative experiences,” Jessica Koravos, CEO of Pophouse Entertainment, said in a statement. “Building on our partnerships with legendary artists and productions, including KISS, Iron Maiden, Tina Turner, Sia, Cyndi Lauper and Avicii, ABBA Voyage, Mamma Mia! The Party and our exhibitions, we aim to carry these legacies to audiences worldwide. Greg and Tina are two of the most accomplished leaders in live entertainment, and they bring exactly the combination of commercial discipline and creative ambition we need for the next chapter. I am delighted to welcome them both to our leadership team.”

Prescription Songs has promoted Caitlin LoPilato to director of A&R. She had previously held roles at Def Jam, Mogul Vision/Arista, 300 Entertainment and Platinum Grammar Publishing.

“Caitlin has been an incredible asset to the team at Prescription Songs, bringing a thoughtful creative perspective and a genuine passion for the artists, songwriters, and producers she works with,” Parsricha Kullas, president of A&R, said in a statement.

Louisa Shipnuck Jones has joined Iron Mountain as vp of media and architectural services.

“We are excited that Louisa will be leading our Media and Archival Services business. She brings a unique blend of experience, from owning the revenue of a premier television library to bringing media technology solutions to studios, broadcasters, news outlets and sports leagues,” Karen Feldman, senior vp and chief marketing officer at Iron Mountain, said in a statement. “Very few people understand our clients’ world the way Louisa does, and that perspective will help them unlock new growth opportunities and greater value from their media assets.”

AdTonos announced the company has rebranded to Turms and will be moving from programmatic audio to Movement Media, which is the company’s agentic media-buying technology.

“For ten years, we’ve shaped the evolution of programmatic audio advertising. But the way people experience media has changed dramatically, and the technology connecting brands with audiences needs to evolve alongside it,” Michael Marcinik, founder and CEO of Turms, said in a statement. “Turms represents our ambition to build on what we’ve established in audio and create something broader: an intelligent infrastructure that understands context as people move through their day. As early as 2019, our first attribution studies using Audiopixel highlighted audio’s ability to influence people’s decisions. But unlocking that potential requires a deliberate role in the media mix, with the right timing and coordination across channels, not simply as an add-on to extend reach.  We believe the future of advertising isn’t about reaching people more often. It’s about understanding when an interaction actually makes sense and this is exactly what Movement Media AI is for.”

David Wilson and Atika Lynch, who both previously served as directors of artist development at Sony Music’s AWAL, have launched cltr;shft, a firm that specializes in digital marketing and audience growth. Wilson serves as of-founder and fractional head of content and strategy at the company and is based in Los Angeles, while Lynch is co-founder and fractional head of audience growth and culture strategy and is based in New York.

#704. Inside Slayyyter’s Big Year: From ‘WOR$T GIRL’ Breakthrough to Best New Artist Grammy Nomination

"Rather than trying to make Slayyyter fit into the mainstream, we focused on bringing the mainstream into her world," says RECORDS' Andrew Saltman.

When Slayyyter released her third album, WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA, in March, she considered it to be her swan song. Her previous two albums, 2021’s Troubled Paradise and 2023’s Starfucker, hadn’t charted on the Billboard 200, and the pop singer admitted in countless interviews that she believed her most recent effort would be her last.

Instead, the reaction was extraordinary. WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA hit No. 22 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on Billboard‘s Top Dance Albums chart. That success was enough to drive Slayyyter to a sold-out tour supporting her album (and the recent announcement that she’ll be headlining Madison Square Garden next June), but her big year didn’t end there. On Monday (Nov. 16), nominations for this year’s Grammys were announced, and Slayyyter received four nods: best new artist, best dance/electronic album, best dance pop recording for her song “DANCE…” and best dance/electronic recording for her song “CRANK.”

To cap off the year, Slayyyter has one final trick up her sleeve: On Dec. 4, she’ll release wor$t man in america, her follow-up to WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA. Rather than a traditional deluxe, the dance-pop artist has chosen to extend the original album’s universe with nine new songs, including its first four singles: “brand new chanel$,” “crank 2,” “i think he’s got a girl” and “hey boyyy.”

All of this has contributed to RECORDS’ Andrew Saltman being named Billboard‘s Executive of the Week. As senior vp of artist development, Saltman helped spearhead Slayyyter’s album (and subsequent Grammy) campaign. He oversaw the marketing and digital strategy for WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA and, now, wor$t man in america. And he attests they’re just getting started.

This week, Slayyyter received four Grammy nominations, including for Best New Artist. What key decision did you make to help make that happen?

What an amazing week for Slayyyter and the entire team. When we first started crafting the campaign around “BEAT UP CHANEL$,” I had a best new artist nomination in the back of my mind. It was certainly a lofty goal, but one I genuinely believed was achievable. I wasn’t necessarily saying that out loud at the time, but I knew we had something special. My focus was on building a campaign that would introduce Slayyyter’s vision to a much broader audience and, in turn, help the industry recognize what she was creating.

The key decision was to commit fully to that vision and build a thoughtful, long-term campaign around it, rather than trying to fit her into an existing industry playbook. I think a big part of my job, particularly at a joint venture label that puts such an emphasis on artist development, is to champion our artists and make believers out of the industry, our partners, and, of course, the fans. I led the overall rollout strategy for WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA from the label side and was very hands-on in bringing it to life alongside our team and partners, always with Slayyyter’s creative vision at the center. She has such a phenomenal creative vision, and I feel strongly that my job is to amplify that vision rather than force certain strategies or perceived best practices onto an artist.

One of the benefits of being at a label like RECORDS is that we’re able to get in the weeds with our artists and their management teams to develop bespoke strategies that work best for each individual artist and campaign. Slayyyter’s management team at Foundations, led by Kenny Consor, and her publicity team at The Oriel have been incredible partners throughout this process. We’re also fortunate to have an amazing partner in Columbia Records, who have supported our decisions and brought their tremendous experience and expertise to the table. Ultimately, these four nominations, especially Best New Artist, are an incredible recognition of Slayyyter’s talent, originality and the years of work she’s put into getting here.

Getting a Best New Artist nomination is a big achievement in a year stacked with rising talent. How did you approach the campaign around not just the dance/electronic categories but the more mainstream categories, including BNA?

From the beginning, we felt strongly that WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA was a project that couldn’t be defined by any one genre. It’s a melting pot of influences, from electronic and dance to pop, rock and even metal. Slayyyter showed an incredible amount of range on this album, and while some of the songs aren’t necessarily what you would consider traditionally commercial records, I actually think that’s what made the project so special and helped it stand out in an exceptionally crowded year.

Our approach was never to build a campaign around fitting into particular Grammy categories or trying to manufacture mainstream appeal. We wanted to embrace everything that made this project unique and introduce Slayyyter to audiences well beyond the dance and electropop scenes. I’ve always believed that great artists push culture forward rather than simply fit the mold of what’s currently popular, and that’s exactly what Slayyyter has done with this album.

One example that really stands out to me is “DANCE…” Slayyyter felt strongly about keeping the song’s long, building intro. Conventional wisdom might suggest getting to the hook as quickly as possible, but we trusted her instincts. Sure enough, that very intro became the sound that went viral on social media and helped turn the song into a cultural phenomenon this year. It’s a perfect example of why I believe in trusting an artist’s creative instincts rather than trying to fit their music into a formula.

She actually put it best in an interview with Billboard earlier this year: “I’m going to make it cool to myself, and not try to make it sound appealing to anyone but me.” I think that mentality is a huge part of why this album has resonated with so many people. Rather than trying to make Slayyyter fit into the mainstream, we focused on bringing the mainstream into her world. To me, the best new artist nomination is a testament to the fact that great artistry can transcend genre.

What was it about Slayyyter that initially drove the decision to sign her?

It really felt like the right place, right time for Slayyyter. She had spent the better part of a decade building an incredibly dedicated fanbase and honing her craft as a songwriter, performer and creative. In many ways, we felt she was hiding in plain sight. All the pieces were there for her to have a major breakthrough, and we recognized an opportunity to help bring what she had already built to an entirely new level.

I distinctly remember sitting in Barry Weiss‘s office with Sabrina Finkelstein, Slayyyter’s A&R, listening to a rough version of “BEAT UP CHANEL$.” Funny enough, the conversation wasn’t initially about Slayyyter, but rather one of her key collaborators, Austin Corona, in connection with Barry’s publishing venture, Bossy Songs. Austin is someone we’re now proud to publish and work closely with. But when we heard that record, we were immediately blown away by its distinct sound, creative direction and authenticity.

I felt I understood exactly what Slayyyter was trying to accomplish creatively, and it was immediately clear to me that she had something incredibly special. We knew we wanted to be in business with her, and ultimately made a deal because we believed so strongly in her potential.

Slayyyter had a fanbase previously, but WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA was her big mainstream breakthrough. How did you approach the campaign for the album to get her to that next level?

From the very beginning, we were focused on two things: starting with making sure we superserved Slayyyter’s core fanbase and stayed true to the DIY ethos that had defined her career. WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA was a sonic departure from her previous albums, so our first priority was ensuring that her existing fans felt just as connected to this new era as they had to everything that came before it. Slayyyter has such an amazing, dedicated fanbase, and their enthusiasm and support became the foundation for everything we built throughout the campaign. From there, we focused on introducing her to an entirely new audience without compromising what made her so special in the first place.

We put a lot of emphasis on creating authentic moments that would resonate with those fans. One of my favorite examples was a small listening event in New York City around the release of “BEAT UP CHANEL$,” where we gave away knockoff Chanel bags that Slayyyter had personally purchased on Canal Street and “beat up” herself. It’s a small detail, but those are the kinds of creative touches that made this campaign so special and helped build a deeper connection between Slayyyter and her audience.

The other major focus was the rollout strategy itself. We deliberately went against the grain of the current industry playbook of quick album campaigns and flooding the market with new music. Instead, we built an eight-month campaign that slowly introduced the world of WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA, giving each release room to breathe and creating meaningful marketing moments along the way. I’ve always liked to describe my approach to marketing as being “proactively reactive.” You need a clear strategy and long-term vision, but you also have to be nimble enough to recognize what’s connecting and adjust accordingly. That approach has been especially important to the digital marketing campaigns we’ve run throughout this rollout.

A great example of that was the visual component of this campaign. We didn’t necessarily set out to create what many fans have described as a visual album, but as the campaign progressed, it became clear just how impactful Slayyyter’s videos were. I made it a priority to ensure that every song had a strong visual supporting it. Slayyyter is an incredibly visual artist, and every one of those music videos is her brainchild. She writes the treatments and directs them herself. She’s truly an artist’s artist, and giving those creative ideas the proper platform and time to resonate became a huge part of our strategy.

By the time WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA arrived at the end of March, just ahead of Coachella, we had spent months building anticipation, expanding her audience and bringing more and more people into Slayyyter’s WOR$T GIRL universe.

She got a lot of buzz from her performances at Coachella and Lollapalooza this year that really seemed to rocket her to a new level of attention. How important do you think those performances were in her breakthrough?

Coachella was a massive moment for Slayyyter. We always felt that the live component was going to be a huge piece of the puzzle, and we had those Coachella dates circled on the calendar from the moment they were confirmed. We knew we had something special, but seeing the crowd overflowing the Mojave tent for an afternoon set was one of the first moments where we could really see everything coming together. It was clear that the music and the campaign were translating into something much bigger, and that we were on the verge of a major breakthrough.

From there, we really leaned into the live performances as key tentpole moments throughout the campaign. Her late-night television debut performing “DANCE…” on The Tonight Show was another enormous milestone. Beyond the national exposure, I think that moment meant so much to the fans who had been supporting her for years. Seeing Slayyyter on that stage felt like a real “she made it” moment, not just for her, but for everyone who had been along for the ride.

The momentum continued throughout the summer festival circuit. At Governor’s Ball, she drew more than 25,000 fans for another afternoon set, roughly doubling the audience we had seen at Coachella. That all culminated in her incredible Lollapalooza performance in front of more than 50,000 people, doubling her festival crowd once again. We also used Lollapalooza as a major moment to launch “brand new chanel$,” the lead single from her forthcoming album, wor$t man in america.

What’s been especially exciting is that these weren’t isolated moments. Each performance built on the last, and the audiences just kept getting bigger. Her agents at THE•TEAM have been phenomenal partners in helping build the touring side of her career as that demand has grown. She’s already been announced for multiple major festivals next year, including headlining slots at some, and I think we’re only beginning to see what Slayyyter is capable of as a live performer.

What are some other highlights from the WOR$T GIRL marketing plan?

One of my personal favorites was our take on the traditional Coachella billboard. The now-infamous “Slayyyter bunny” had become a recurring character in this campaign, and in keeping with Slayyyter’s DIY ethos, we decided to do something a little different. Rather than putting up a traditional billboard along the highway to Indio, like so many major artists do, we had multiple bunnies standing on the side of the road holding signs promoting her set and album. The stunt ended up making multiple best Coachella billboard lists, including taking the top spot on Paste Magazine‘s ranking.

Another key element was the dollar sign. It’s such a simple motif, but we used it consistently throughout the campaign to the point where a dollar sign became synonymous with the WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA era. It’s a great example of how something so simple can become an incredibly recognizable part of an artist’s identity when executed consistently.

Lastly, I loved the limited-edition dirt-filled vinyl we created for WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA. It was a nod to the dirt and mud that appear throughout the “BEAT UP CHANEL$” music video and a unique way to bring the visual world of the album into a physical product.

Slayyyter has a follow-up album, wor$t man in america, scheduled for a Dec. 4 release. It’s a quick follow-up to WOR$T GIRL, which was only released in March — was there an intentional push to get the new album out this year to capitalize on the attention she’s been receiving?

That was certainly a consideration when putting together the wor$t man in america campaign, but it was only one contributing factor. We always felt that the WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA campaign would really hit its stride once the full album was out and Slayyyter started touring. As we watched everything unfold, it became clear that she was only just getting started and there was so much more of this world to explore.

I don’t want to speak for Slayyyter creatively, but as a fan and listener, I genuinely felt she was writing some of her best material yet following the release of WOR$T GIRL. Songs like the recently released “hey boyyy” and “brand new chanel$” are perfect examples of that. “brand new chanel$” in particular felt different from the very first listen, and that feeling has only grown as we’ve watched it connect with audiences, especially in her live show. It’s such a massive, anthemic record that resonates with so many people, and it continues to reach new heights. I really believe in that song, and our entire team is doing everything we can to help it reach its full potential.

Of course, Slayyyter is always doing things her own way, and the idea of an inverse album, a true “brother” album to WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA, was entirely hers. A traditional deluxe album filled with remixes and features just didn’t feel right for a project this unique. What I love about the concept is that it gave us an opportunity to continue building on the world we had established while introducing an entirely new creative chapter. Even the visual identity has been inverted, swapping the signature red of WOR$T GIRL for cyan on wor$t man, while carrying over familiar imagery and motifs from the original campaign. That same approach has extended into the marketing, allowing us to build on the momentum with new music, visuals and creative moments that feel fresh while remaining connected to everything that came before. I think wor$t man in america is the perfect way to put a bow on this sonic era.

Slayyyter has achieved a lot of big milestones this year — what are your hopes for 2027?

A couple of Grammys, platinum singles and albums and Slayyyter becoming an established arena-level act. Not too much to ask for, I don’t think!

In all seriousness, my hope for 2027 is to continue establishing Slayyyter as a global superstar, regardless of what our release schedule looks like next year. We’ve accomplished so much in 2026, but I genuinely believe we’re only scratching the surface of what’s possible for her. There’s an incredible opportunity to build on this momentum, continue expanding her audience around the world and introduce even more people to her music. Ultimately, we’ll continue doing what got us here in the first place: supporting Slayyyter’s creative vision and amplifying her immense talent.
